title: The Song of Moses and the Lamb; the Bowl Angels Go Out
summary: John sees a third great sign in heaven: seven angels holding the seven last plagues that complete God's wrath. Before the plagues fall, the people who overcame the beast stand beside a sea of glass mixed with fire and sing a new Exodus hymn, the song of Moses and of the Lamb, which celebrates God's justice and looks for all nations to come and worship. The heavenly sanctuary, called the tabernacle of the testimony, opens. Seven angels dressed like priests come out, receive seven golden bowls of wrath from one of the living creatures, and the temple fills with smoke of God's glory so that no one can enter until the plagues are finished. The chapter is a short liturgical prelude that frames the bowl judgments as holy, covenantal and just.

outline.heading: The third great sign: seven angels with the last plagues
The conquerors by the sea of glass sing the song of Moses and the Lamb
The tabernacle of the testimony opens; seven priestly angels come out
A living creature hands over seven golden bowls of wrath
Smoke of glory fills the temple; no one may enter

context:
Chapter 15 is built from the Exodus story. The seven last plagues echo the plagues on Egypt (Exodus 7-12); the victors standing by a sea echo Israel on the shore of the Red Sea (Exodus 14:30-15:1); their hymn is named after the song Moses sang there (Exodus 15) and also uses Deuteronomy 32, the second song of Moses, which speaks of God's ways as just and true. Yet the words of the hymn are drawn mostly from the Psalms and Prophets (Psalm 86:9; 98:1-2; 111:2; 145:17; Jeremiah 10:7; Malachi 1:11), which look for the nations to worship Israel's God. The scene is also a temple scene. The "tabernacle of the testimony" was the wilderness tent that housed the tablets of the covenant (Exodus 38:21; Numbers 1:50), and the cloud that fills it recalls the dedication of the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34-35) and of Solomon's temple (1 Kings 8:10-11), when the priests could not go in. The angels' linen and golden sashes are priestly dress, and the bowls (Greek phialai) are the shallow libation and incense bowls of temple service (Exodus 25:29; Numbers 7). Ezekiel 9-10, where a man in linen receives coals from a cherub to scatter over Jerusalem, is a close pattern for 15:6-7.

For readers in Asia Minor the scene stood against the setting of the imperial cult. Cities such as Ephesus, Pergamum and Smyrna sang hymns to the emperor in temple choirs (hymnodoi) and hailed him as lord and saviour; the hymn here gives the titles "Lord God Almighty" and "King of the nations" to God alone. The structural question is disputed: many read the bowls as a final, intensified retelling of the seals and trumpets (recapitulation), while others read them as the last in a sequence of events. The chapter is also linked to 14:1-5 (the 144,000 with harps) and 12:1-3 (the first two great signs).

symbols.phrase: Another great and marvellous sign in heaven
symbols.jewish: Greek semeion picks up the "great sign" of the woman (Revelation 12:1) and the "other sign" of the dragon (12:3); this is the third. "Signs and wonders" is Exodus vocabulary for the plagues on Egypt (Exodus 7:3; Deuteronomy 4:34; Psalm 78:43), and "great and marvellous" anticipates the hymn of 15:3 (Psalm 111:2; 139:14).
symbols.cultural: In Greco-Roman culture portents (signa, prodigia) in the sky were read as messages about the fate of rulers; Revelation claims the decisive signs come from the throne of God.
symbols.meaning: The word marks a major new unit. The first sign showed the people of God, the second their enemy, and the third God's answer: judgment that completes his wrath. Most interpreters see 15:1 as a heading for the whole bowl section, with 15:2-8 as its prelude.

symbols.phrase: Seven angels with the seven final plagues, completing God's wrath
symbols.jewish: The plagues on Egypt (Exodus 7-12) are the master pattern, and the number seven recalls the covenant curses of Leviticus 26, where God warns four times that he will punish Israel "seven times" for her sins (Leviticus 26:18, 21, 24, 28). "Wrath is completed" (Greek etelesthe) echoes the idea of a measure of sin filled up (Genesis 15:16; Daniel 8:23; 1 Thessalonians 2:16).
symbols.meaning: The bowls are "last" because with them God's wrath reaches its goal. Whether "last" means last in time (after the seals and trumpets) or last in John's sequence of visions (a final, most intense retelling) is one of the main structural disputes in Revelation. The bowls are total where the trumpets were partial (a third), suggesting escalation.

readings.reading: The seven last plagues are the covenant curses of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28 falling on apostate Jerusalem in the Jewish War (AD 66-70); "last" means the end of the old covenant order (Chilton, Gentry).
The bowls follow the trumpets in time; classic historicists (Elliott, Barnes) placed them from the French Revolution (1789) onward as judgments on papal Rome and its supporters.
The bowls are the final, rapid judgments at the very end of the future seven-year tribulation, just before Christ returns (Walvoord, Thomas). They come out of the seventh trumpet.
The bowls retell the same age-long story as the seals and trumpets, but from the angle of final, unrestricted judgment on the impenitent (Hendriksen's "progressive parallelism").
Beale reads the bowls as recapitulating the trumpets and focusing on the climax of history, while allowing that they also describe judgments through the church age.

symbols.phrase: A sea of glass mixed with fire
symbols.jewish: The sea of glass first appears before the throne in Revelation 4:6, drawing on the crystal expanse above the cherubim (Ezekiel 1:22), the waters above the firmament (Genesis 1:7; Psalm 104:3) and the bronze "sea" in Solomon's temple court (1 Kings 7:23-26). Here it is mixed with fire, and the conquerors stand by it like Israel on the shore after crossing the Red Sea (Exodus 14:30-15:1). In Jewish tradition the sea was also a symbol of chaos and evil (Psalm 74:13; Daniel 7:2-3), the place from which the beast rose (Revelation 13:1).
symbols.cultural: Glass in the first century was costly and often cloudy; a sea of perfectly clear glass suggests splendour and calm.
symbols.meaning: The sea of chaos and evil has been subdued, and the redeemed stand safely on its shore as Israel did after the Exodus. The fire probably points to the judgment that is about to fall (as it fell on Egypt), or to the fiery trial through which the saints passed. The Greek "epi" can mean "on" or "beside"; many translations prefer "beside" to fit the Red Sea picture.

symbols.phrase: Those who had conquered the beast, its image and the number of its name
symbols.jewish: "Conquering" (Greek nikao) runs through the promises to the seven churches (Revelation 2:7, 11, 17, 26; 3:5, 12, 21) and the victory of the martyrs over the dragon "by the blood of the Lamb" (12:11). Refusing the image recalls Daniel's friends, who would not bow to Nebuchadnezzar's statue (Daniel 3), and the Maccabean martyrs (2 Maccabees 7; 4 Maccabees).
symbols.cultural: In the Roman world "victory" (Nike, Victoria) belonged to the emperor and was celebrated with triumphs and coins. Christians who refused emperor worship looked defeated; John calls them the true victors.
symbols.meaning: The victors are believers who stayed faithful under pressure to worship the beast (Revelation 13:15-17), whether or not they died. Victory means faithful witness, not military force, following the pattern of the Lamb who conquered by being slain (5:5-6).

readings.reading: Primarily tribulation saints, many of them martyrs, who refused the future Antichrist's mark (Walvoord).
All faithful believers of every age who refuse to give their ultimate loyalty to idolatrous power.
First-century Christians who stood firm through the Neronic persecution and the Jewish War.

symbols.phrase: Harps of God
symbols.jewish: The kithara (lyre) was a temple instrument used by the Levitical musicians (1 Chronicles 25:1-6; Psalm 33:2; 150:3). The elders hold harps in Revelation 5:8 and the 144,000 sing with the sound of harps in 14:2. "Harps of God" means instruments given for God's worship (compare 1 Chronicles 16:42, "instruments for the songs of God").
symbols.cultural: The lyre was the instrument of Apollo and of civic hymn choirs, including the choirs that sang to the emperor in Asia.
symbols.meaning: The victors take up the role of the temple singers. Worship, not battle, is their response to victory, and their song interprets the judgments that follow.

symbols.phrase: The song of God's servant Moses and of the Lamb
symbols.jewish: Moses sang after the Red Sea deliverance (Exodus 15:1-18) and taught Israel a second song before his death (Deuteronomy 32), which says God's works are perfect and his ways just and true (Deuteronomy 32:4). "Servant of God" is Moses' title (Exodus 14:31; Joshua 14:7). The hymn's lines are woven from Psalm 86:9-10, 98:1-2, 111:2, 139:14, 145:17, Jeremiah 10:7 and Malachi 1:11. Later rabbinic sources say the Levites sang portions of Deuteronomy 32 at the Sabbath additional offering (Babylonian Talmud Rosh Hashanah 31a; a later tradition), and Exodus 15 became part of daily synagogue prayer.
symbols.cultural: Cities of Asia had hymn-singing guilds that praised the emperor and Roma; this hymn assigns every royal and divine title to God and the Lamb.
symbols.meaning: One song, not two: the Exodus song is now sung as the song of the Lamb, because the Lamb's death is the new Passover and new Exodus. Remarkably, the hymn does not celebrate the enemy's destruction but God's justice and the coming worship of all nations (Bauckham). It interprets the bowls before they fall: they are righteous acts that reveal God to the world.

readings.reading: The hymn's expectation that "all nations will come and worship" anticipates the conversion of the nations through the gospel in history (Psalm 86:9 understood as a promise for this age).
The song looks to the consummation, when the redeemed from every nation worship together; it is also sung now by faith.
Sung by tribulation martyrs; the nations' worship is fulfilled in the millennial kingdom after Christ returns (Zechariah 14:16).

symbols.phrase: O Lord God Almighty
symbols.jewish: Greek pantokrator translates the Hebrew "LORD of hosts" (YHWH Sabaoth) and "God of hosts" in the Septuagint (for example Amos 4:13; Hosea 12:5; Zechariah 1:3). It is one of Revelation's favourite names for God (1:8; 4:8; 11:17; 16:7, 14; 19:6, 15; 21:22).
symbols.cultural: Domitian is reported to have liked being called "our lord and god" (Suetonius, Domitian 13), and emperors bore the title autokrator. The title Almighty denies that any emperor rules the world.
symbols.meaning: God commands every power in heaven and on earth; the plagues that follow are under his authority, not the beast's.

symbols.phrase: Just and true are your ways, King of the nations
symbols.jewish: Jeremiah 10:7 asks who would not fear the "King of the nations"; Deuteronomy 32:4 calls God just and true. The manuscripts differ: some read "King of the ages" (compare 1 Timothy 1:17; Tobit 13:6, 10) and a few "King of the saints"; "nations" has strong support and fits the next verse.
symbols.cultural: Roman emperors presented themselves as rulers of the "inhabited world" (oikoumene) and guardians of justice (iustitia); the hymn locates true justice and universal kingship in God.
symbols.meaning: God's judgments are not arbitrary or vindictive; they are consistent with his character and his covenant. His rule extends over every people, not just Israel or the church.

symbols.phrase: All nations will come and worship before you
symbols.jewish: Psalm 86:9 is quoted almost directly; the pilgrimage of the nations to Zion is a major prophetic hope (Isaiah 2:2-4; 66:23; Zechariah 8:20-23; 14:16, at the Feast of Tabernacles). Jewish writings of the period share it (Tobit 13:11; 1 Enoch 90:30-33; Psalms of Solomon 17:31).
symbols.meaning: God's judgments are meant to reveal him so that the nations fear and glorify him. Interpreters disagree whether this means genuine conversion of the nations (Bauckham sees Revelation's hope for the nations as remarkably broad), or the final acknowledgment, willing or not, of God's rule (Philippians 2:10-11).

readings.reading: Points to the large-scale conversion of the nations in history before Christ returns, as the gospel triumphs.
Fulfilled in the gathering of the redeemed from every nation throughout this age and perfected at the consummation (Revelation 21:24-26).
Fulfilled in the millennial kingdom when the nations go up to Jerusalem to worship (Zechariah 14:16).
Expresses the universal goal of God's judgments in every era: to bring people to recognise him.

symbols.phrase: The temple, the tabernacle of the Testimony, opened in heaven
symbols.jewish: The "tent of the testimony" was the wilderness tabernacle, named for the tablets of the Ten Commandments in the ark (Exodus 38:21; 40:20; Numbers 1:50-53; 17:7; Acts 7:44). Moses built it after the heavenly pattern (Exodus 25:9, 40; Hebrews 8:5; Wisdom 9:8). Revelation 11:19 earlier showed the ark in the heavenly temple. In Ezekiel 10, judgment on Jerusalem proceeds from the sanctuary.
symbols.meaning: Judgment flows from God's covenant law. The "testimony" is the covenant document; the plagues are the sanctions of a covenant broken. The Exodus wilderness setting continues the new Exodus theme.

readings.reading: A covenant lawsuit: the law that Israel was given is now the ground of judgment on the generation that rejected the Messiah (Chilton).
The heavenly sanctuary is the literal source of the final judgments on a rebellious world at the end of the tribulation.
God's holy law stands behind all his judgments in history; nothing he does is arbitrary.

symbols.phrase: Clean, bright linen and golden sashes around their chests
symbols.jewish: Linen was priestly dress (Exodus 28:39-42), especially the plain linen of the high priest on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:4, 23). The angel in Daniel 10:5 wears linen and a gold belt, and in Ezekiel 9:2-3 a man clothed in linen goes out with the executioners to judge Jerusalem, beginning at the sanctuary. Jesus wears a golden sash in Revelation 1:13. Some manuscripts read "stone" (lithon) for "linen" (linon), perhaps recalling the jewels of Ezekiel 28:13.
symbols.cultural: Fine linen was a luxury in the Roman world; the same word recurs in Babylon's finery (18:12, 16), creating a contrast between holy and corrupt splendour.
symbols.meaning: The angels are priests of the heavenly temple. Their judgment is holy service, not mere violence. The link to Ezekiel 9 suggests judgment beginning at God's house.

readings.reading: The Ezekiel 9 pattern shows that the target is Jerusalem: as in 586 BC, priestly figures carry out judgment on the city and its temple.
Holy angels who will execute the final judgments on the earth; the clothing marks their purity.

symbols.phrase: One of the four living creatures gave the seven angels seven golden bowls
symbols.jewish: The phialai were the broad, shallow bowls used in the tabernacle and temple for incense and for libations or blood (Exodus 25:29; 27:3; Numbers 7:13-86; 1 Kings 7:50). In Revelation 5:8 the same golden bowls hold incense, the prayers of the saints. The cup of God's wrath is a prophetic image (Isaiah 51:17, 22; Jeremiah 25:15-29). In Ezekiel 10:6-7 a cherub hands burning coals to the man in linen to scatter over Jerusalem.
symbols.cultural: In Greek religion the phiale was the standard libation bowl, shown on vases and statues in the hands of gods and worshippers.
symbols.meaning: The bowls that once carried the prayers of the saints (5:8; 6:10; 8:3-5) now carry God's answer to those prayers. A living creature, guardian of the throne, hands them over: judgment comes from the very presence of God.

symbols.phrase: The temple filled with smoke; no one could enter
symbols.jewish: When the tabernacle was finished, the cloud covered it and Moses could not enter (Exodus 40:34-35); at Solomon's dedication the priests could not minister because of the cloud (1 Kings 8:10-11); Isaiah saw the temple filled with smoke (Isaiah 6:4). In Ezekiel 10:3-4 the cloud fills the temple court just before the glory departs from Jerusalem.
symbols.meaning: God's presence in holiness and power is so intense that none may approach. Many interpreters take it to mean that the time for intercession has passed: the judgments are fixed and will run their full course.

readings.reading: Recalls the departure of the glory from the earthly temple in Ezekiel 10; the old sanctuary is about to be destroyed (AD 70).
Marks a point late in the tribulation after which no intercession halts the final plagues.
There comes a point in every rebellion, and finally at the last judgment, when God's patience gives way to judgment.

The bowl angels come from the tabernacle of the covenant to execute the sevenfold covenant curses (Leviticus 26) on first-century Jerusalem. The pattern of Ezekiel 9-10, where judgment begins at the sanctuary and the glory departs, is applied to the Jewish War of AD 66-70. The song of Moses and the Lamb is sung by Christians delivered from the old order, the new Israel after a new Exodus (Chilton, Gentry).

Agrees that the bowls fell on old-covenant Israel in AD 66-70 and adds that this judgment was the consummation itself: the end of the old covenant age, the Second Coming in judgment and the full opening of the heavenly sanctuary (Hebrews 9:8). Critics note that this view denies a future bodily return and resurrection affirmed by the historic creeds; proponents reply that the creeds must yield to the time-texts of Scripture.

The bowls follow the trumpets in history. Elliott and Barnes saw the chapter as the preparation for judgments on papal Europe beginning with the French Revolution; the conquerors are the faithful witnesses who resisted the papacy (the beast) through the centuries.

The chapter introduces the final judgments of the future tribulation, which come in rapid succession just before Christ returns. The singers are tribulation believers, many martyred, who refused the Antichrist's mark. Dispensationalists see the bowls as the content of the seventh trumpet (Walvoord, Thomas).

The bowls retell the whole age from the perspective of final, unrestricted judgment. The chapter's message is that God's judgments are holy, just and covenantal, and that the faithful who refuse idolatry will stand victorious and sing (Hendriksen, Milligan).

Beale and Osborne combine readings: the vision applies to the church's conflict with Rome and every later "beast", and culminates in the final judgment. The bowls recapitulate the trumpets but go further, reaching the end.

questions: Why does the hymn in 15:3-4 celebrate God's justice and the worship of the nations rather than the destruction of enemies? What does that suggest about the purpose of the bowls?
How does the Exodus pattern (plagues, sea, song, tabernacle) shape the way the bowl judgments should be read?
What difference does it make whether the bowls are read as following the trumpets in time or as retelling them?
The bowls that held the saints' prayers (5:8) now hold wrath. What does this suggest about prayer and justice?

title: The Seven Bowls of Wrath and Armageddon
summary: A voice from the temple sends the seven angels to pour out their bowls. The first four strike the earth, sea, rivers and sun in a pattern that follows the first four trumpets and the plagues of Egypt, but now without limit: sores, the sea and rivers turned to blood, scorching heat. The angel of the waters and the altar declare these judgments just, because the oppressors shed the blood of saints and prophets. The fifth bowl darkens the beast's throne; the sixth dries up the Euphrates for the kings of the east while three froglike spirits gather the kings of the world for the battle of the great day of God at Armageddon. The seventh bowl, poured into the air, brings the cry "It is done", the greatest earthquake, the splitting of the great city, the fall of Babylon and enormous hail, yet people still curse God rather than repent.

outline.heading: The command from the temple
First bowl: sores on the beast's worshippers
Second bowl: the sea becomes blood
Third bowl: rivers and springs become blood; the angel of the waters and the altar affirm God's justice
Fourth bowl: the sun scorches; no repentance
Fifth bowl: darkness on the throne of the beast
Sixth bowl: the Euphrates dried; frog spirits gather the kings to Armageddon; the thief saying
Seventh bowl: "It is done"; earthquake, the great city split, Babylon judged, giant hail

context:
The bowls are a new set of Exodus plagues. Sores (Exodus 9:8-12), water turned to blood (7:17-21), darkness (10:21-23), frogs (8:1-15), and hail with thunder (9:22-26) all come from the Egyptian plagues, and the drying of waters for a people to cross recalls the Red Sea and the Jordan. The order of the first four bowls (earth, sea, rivers, sun) matches the first four trumpets (8:7-12), but the trumpets struck a third while the bowls are total. Jewish reflection on the plagues had already drawn the lesson that God punishes people "by the very things by which they sin" (Wisdom of Solomon 11:5-16; 16-19), which explains the "blood for blood" logic of 16:6. Deuteronomy 28 threatens Israel with "the boils of Egypt" if it breaks the covenant (Deuteronomy 28:27, 60), a point preterists stress. The gathering of the nations to battle on "the great day" uses Joel 3, Zechariah 12-14 and Ezekiel 38-39.

In the Roman East, the Euphrates was the frontier with the Parthian empire, Rome's feared rival, whose mounted archers had defeated Roman armies (Carrhae, 53 BC; the surrender at Rhandeia, AD 62). After Nero's death in AD 68 rumours spread that he would return from the east at the head of Parthian armies (Tacitus, Histories 2.8; Suetonius, Nero 57; Sibylline Oracles 4.119-139 and 5.137-154). The cities of Asia had also suffered great earthquakes (twelve cities destroyed in AD 17; Laodicea in AD 60), so the final earthquake would strike a nerve. The interpretive questions are sharp: is the "great city" Jerusalem, Rome or a future capital; is Armageddon a literal valley, a symbolic name or a mountain; and do the bowls describe the end of the age or judgments within history?

symbols.phrase: Go, pour out on the earth the seven bowls of God's wrath
symbols.jewish: The prophets ask God to "pour out" his wrath on the nations (Psalm 69:24; 79:6; Jeremiah 10:25; Zephaniah 3:8) and threaten it on unfaithful Israel (Ezekiel 7:8; 14:19; 22:31). In temple ritual priests poured out the blood of sin offerings at the base of the altar (Leviticus 4:7, 18). The loud voice from the temple is probably God himself (Isaiah 66:6: "a voice from the temple, the voice of the LORD repaying his enemies").
symbols.cultural: Pouring a libation from a phiale was a standard act of Greek and Roman worship; here the libation is wrath.
symbols.meaning: Judgment is pictured as a liturgical act carried out from the sanctuary by priestly angels at God's command.

symbols.phrase: Loathsome, malignant sores on those with the mark of the beast
symbols.jewish: The sixth Egyptian plague brought festering boils on people and animals (Exodus 9:8-12). Deuteronomy 28:27, 35 threatens Israel with "the boils of Egypt" for covenant breaking; Job was struck with sores (Job 2:7).
symbols.cultural: Those marked for the beast perhaps bore a visible sign of allegiance; now they bear a visible mark of judgment. Skin diseases carried shame and exclusion in the ancient world.
symbols.meaning: The judgment fits the sin: those who took the beast's mark receive God's mark of judgment. The plague strikes only the beast's worshippers, as the Egyptian plagues spared Israel (Exodus 9:26).

readings.reading: The Deuteronomy 28 curse of the "boils of Egypt" falls on apostate Israel in the last years before AD 70 (Chilton).
Elliott linked it to the moral and social ulcer of atheism and revolution that broke out in papal France from 1789.
A literal, painful epidemic affecting only those who took the Antichrist's mark in the future tribulation.
The inner and outer misery that idolatry brings on those who give themselves to it.

symbols.phrase: The sea turned to blood like that of the dead
keywords: blood like that of the dead
symbols.jewish: The first Egyptian plague turned the Nile to blood and killed the fish (Exodus 7:17-21). The second trumpet turned a third of the sea to blood (Revelation 8:8-9); now all the sea is struck. "Like the blood of a dead man" suggests congealed, corrupt blood.
symbols.cultural: The Mediterranean was the artery of Roman trade and grain supply (the merchants and sailors of chapter 18 depend on it), so a dead sea threatens the economy of the empire.
symbols.meaning: The source of life and wealth becomes a source of death. The universality ("every living thing") marks the bowls as final and complete compared with the trumpets.

readings.reading: Chilton points to Josephus' description of the naval slaughter of Jews on the Sea of Galilee near Tarichaeae in AD 67, when the water was red with blood and full of corpses (Jewish War 3.522-531).
Applied to the great naval wars of 1793-1815 that destroyed the fleets and maritime commerce of France and its allies.
A literal, global death of marine life in the future tribulation.
Represents judgments that strike the commercial and economic life of godless society.

symbols.phrase: Rivers and springs of water turned to blood
symbols.jewish: Exodus 7:19-24 (all Egypt's water turned to blood); Psalm 78:44 and 105:29 recall it. The third trumpet had made a third of the rivers bitter (Revelation 8:10-11).
symbols.cultural: Cities depended on springs and aqueducts; contaminated water meant disease and death.
symbols.meaning: Fresh water, necessary for life, becomes undrinkable. The next verses explain the logic: those who shed blood are given blood to drink.

readings.reading: Josephus describes the Jordan choked with corpses after the slaughter of refugees from Gadara (Jewish War 4.433-437); preterists see the land's waters defiled by the war.

Elliott and others applied it to the wars of the 1790s in the Alpine and Italian river valleys, regions where Waldensian and other dissenters had been persecuted, so that the land "drank blood" for blood it had shed.
A literal, worldwide contamination of fresh water during the tribulation.

symbols.phrase: The angel of the waters: Righteous are You, O Holy One, who is and was
symbols.jewish: Jewish apocalyptic assigned angels to elements of creation: angels of the winds, clouds, snow and waters (Jubilees 2:2; 1 Enoch 60:11-22; 66:1-2; compare Revelation 7:1; 14:18). Confessing God's justice when judgment falls is a known form (a "doxology of judgment"): Deuteronomy 32:4; Psalm 119:137; Prayer of Azariah (Daniel 3:27 in the Greek); Tobit 3:2.
symbols.meaning: Even the angel responsible for the waters agrees that their ruin is just. God is called the One "who is and who was" without "who is to come" (as in 11:17), because in these judgments he has come.

symbols.phrase: They spilled the blood of saints and prophets, and You gave them blood to drink
symbols.jewish: Isaiah 49:26 says the oppressors will be drunk with their own blood. Wisdom of Solomon 11:6-7 interprets the Nile plague as a fitting punishment for Pharaoh's decree to drown Hebrew infants, and states the principle that one is punished by the means of one's sin (11:16). Jesus charged Jerusalem with the blood of the prophets and said it would come on "this generation" (Matthew 23:29-36; Luke 11:47-51).
symbols.cultural: Roman executions of Christians under Nero (Tacitus, Annals 15.44) were recent memory if Revelation was written either in the 60s or the 90s.
symbols.meaning: Strict justice (lex talionis): punishment fits the crime. The killers of God's witnesses are made to "drink" blood. "As they deserve" (Greek axioi eisin) is a stark contrast with the Lamb, who is "worthy" (axios) in 5:9.

readings.reading: Applies to Jerusalem, which Jesus said had killed the prophets and on which all the righteous blood would come within that generation (Matthew 23:35-36; Luke 13:33).
Refers to the persecutors of tribulation saints in the end-time, who receive just retribution.
A permanent principle: persecuting powers in every age reap what they sow.

symbols.phrase: The altar replies: Yes, Lord God Almighty, true and just are Your judgments
symbols.jewish: The souls of the martyrs cried out from under the altar for vindication (Revelation 6:9-10); the prayers of the saints rose from the golden altar and fire from it was thrown to the earth (8:3-5); a voice came from the altar's horns (9:13). Blood poured at the altar's base (Leviticus 4:7) gives the image its force.
symbols.meaning: The altar, standing for the martyrs and the prayers of the saints, confirms that the long cry "How long?" has been answered justly. The double witness (angel and altar) follows the legal rule of two witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15).

symbols.phrase: The sun given power to scorch people with fire
symbols.jewish: Deuteronomy 32:24 threatens "burning heat"; Malachi 4:1 speaks of a day burning like an oven. It reverses the promise to the redeemed that the sun will not strike them (Isaiah 49:10; Revelation 7:16). The fourth trumpet darkened a third of the sun (8:12).
symbols.cultural: In the hot climate of Asia and Judea, heat and drought meant crop failure and death; sun worship (Sol Invictus later, Helios and Apollo in the first century) was widespread.
symbols.meaning: Creation itself turns against those who worship the creature. The fourth bowl reverses the protection promised to the sealed people of God.

readings.reading: Barnes and Elliott applied it to the devastating wars of Napoleon, which "scorched" Europe, especially the papal and Catholic powers.
A literal intensification of solar heat in the last days.
Judgment through the natural order, which in every age can become a scourge on rebellious people.

symbols.phrase: They cursed the name of God and did not repent and give Him glory
symbols.jewish: Pharaoh hardened his heart after each plague (Exodus 8:15, 32; 9:34-35). Amos 4:6-11 repeats after each disaster "yet you did not return to me". Contrast Revelation 11:13, where survivors give glory to God, and 15:4, where nations fear and glorify him.
symbols.cultural: Cursing gods in misfortune was known in antiquity; blasphemy here echoes the beast's own blasphemies (13:5-6).
symbols.meaning: The plagues are not only punitive but also a call to repent, yet hardened people refuse. The repeated refrain shows that suffering alone does not change hearts, and justifies the final judgment.

readings.reading: A picture of the hardening that sets in whenever people persist in idolatry; judgment exposes rather than changes the heart.
Describes the attitude of the unbelieving world in the final days of the tribulation.

symbols.phrase: Bowl on the throne of the beast: its kingdom plunged into darkness
symbols.jewish: The ninth Egyptian plague brought a darkness that could be felt (Exodus 10:21-23); Wisdom of Solomon 17 elaborates it as a darkness of terror and guilt. The prophets speak of darkness on the day of the LORD (Joel 2:2; Amos 5:18-20; Isaiah 60:2). The dragon gave the beast his throne (Revelation 13:2).
symbols.cultural: The "throne" points to the seat of imperial power. The Roman world experienced the near-collapse of the empire in the civil wars of AD 68-69 (the year of four emperors), after Nero's suicide.
symbols.meaning: God strikes the centre of the beast's power. Darkness signals confusion, collapse of authority and despair.

readings.reading: Rome's chaos in AD 68-69, when Nero died and rival emperors fought, so that the beast's kingdom was plunged into darkness (Gentry; Chilton relates it more to Jerusalem's distress).
The humiliation of the papal see (the beast's throne) when French armies occupied Rome and took Pope Pius VI captive (1798), followed by the Napoleonic suppression of papal power.
Supernatural darkness over the Antichrist's capital and empire near the end of the tribulation (Walvoord).
Every godless regime eventually experiences the breakdown of its power, a foretaste of final judgment.

symbols.phrase: Men gnawed their tongues in anguish
symbols.jewish: Compare "weeping and gnashing of teeth" in the teaching of Jesus (Matthew 8:12; 13:42) and the anguish in darkness of Wisdom of Solomon 17.
symbols.meaning: A vivid image of agony and helpless rage. Together with "pains and sores" it shows that the bowls accumulate rather than replace one another.

symbols.phrase: The great river Euphrates dried up
symbols.jewish: The Euphrates was the northern boundary of the promised land (Genesis 15:18) and the river of Babylon and Assyria, from beyond which invaders came (Isaiah 8:7; Jeremiah 46:10). God dried waters for his people at the Red Sea (Exodus 14) and the Jordan (Joshua 3), and promised to dry the river again (Isaiah 11:15-16; 44:27; Jeremiah 50:38; 51:36). Cyrus took Babylon by diverting the Euphrates (Herodotus 1.191; Xenophon, Cyropaedia 7.5). The sixth trumpet released angels bound at the Euphrates (Revelation 9:14).
symbols.cultural: For Rome the Euphrates was the frontier with Parthia, the one power Rome feared. The Nero redivivus legend imagined Nero returning from beyond the Euphrates with Parthian armies to destroy Rome (Sibylline Oracles 4.119-139; 5.137-154).
symbols.meaning: A barrier that held back invading armies is removed by God himself. The Cyrus story shows Babylon's fall coming through the drying of its river, so the image prepares for Babylon's judgment in 16:19.

readings.reading: Gentry and Chilton note that Titus' army included troops drawn from the Euphrates frontier and from eastern client kings (Josephus, Jewish War 5.40-46; Tacitus, Histories 5.1): the way was opened for armies to come against Jerusalem.
The drying up of the Ottoman (Turkish) empire that ruled the Euphrates region, a decline that historicists from the 1820s onward identified and watched (Elliott, Barnes).
A literal drying of the Euphrates (perhaps aided by dams) that lets eastern armies march toward Israel for Armageddon (Walvoord).
God removes the restraints on evil so that the forces of the world gather for their final defeat; Babylon falls as it did to Cyrus.

symbols.phrase: The kings of the East
symbols.jewish: Literally "the kings from the rising of the sun". Cyrus is the one "from the east" whom God calls against Babylon (Isaiah 41:2, 25; 46:11). In Revelation 7:2 the sealing angel comes from the rising of the sun.
symbols.cultural: Parthian rulers styled themselves "king of kings" and were the classic eastern threat; their invasion was a stock fear of the Roman East.
symbols.meaning: Eastern rulers coming to make war. Most read them as hostile forces drawn into the final battle; a minority reading (some idealists, following the Cyrus typology) sees them as instruments of God against Babylon, or even as Christ and his people.

readings.reading: Roman generals and eastern client kings (Agrippa II, Antiochus of Commagene, Sohaemus of Emesa, Malchus of Arabia) who joined Vespasian and Titus against Jerusalem.
Variously the converted Jews or Eastern peoples whose way is opened by the decline of Islam, in preparation for Christ's kingdom.
A literal coalition of Asian nations, often connected with the 200 million of Revelation 9:16 (Walvoord).
Nations hostile to God whom he allows to gather; in the Cyrus pattern they also become agents of Babylon's downfall.

symbols.phrase: Three unclean spirits like frogs from the mouths of the dragon, the beast and the false prophet
symbols.jewish: The second Egyptian plague filled the land with frogs (Exodus 8:1-15; Psalm 78:45; 105:30). Frogs were unclean animals (Leviticus 11:9-12, 41-42). Lying spirits that entice kings to battle recall 1 Kings 22:19-23, where a deceiving spirit lures Ahab to his death.
symbols.cultural: In Zoroastrian (Persian) belief, frogs were among the noxious creatures of the evil spirit. Ancient writers mocked the croaking of frogs as empty noise.
symbols.meaning: Three spirits from three mouths form an unholy trinity of propaganda. They come from mouths because their power is deceptive speech that gathers the kings. They are demonic, working signs (compare 13:13-14).

readings.reading: The lying propaganda that drew the Jewish rebels and the nations into the war of AD 66-70, including false prophets who promised deliverance (Josephus, Jewish War 6.285-288).

Nineteenth-century historicists identified three spreading influences of their day; Elliott linked them to infidelity, popery and a priestly sacramentalism, while others named paganism, papalism and Islam.
Literal demonic emissaries who perform miracles to draw world leaders to Armageddon.
The ideologies, lies and propaganda by which evil powers in every age mobilise the world against God and his people.

symbols.phrase: The false prophet
symbols.jewish: Named here for the first time, the false prophet is the beast from the land (Revelation 13:11-17; see 19:20; 20:10). Deuteronomy 13:1-5 warns against prophets who work signs to lead Israel to other gods; Jesus warned of false prophets performing signs (Matthew 24:11, 24).
symbols.cultural: The land beast resembles the provincial priesthood of the imperial cult in Asia, the councils and high priests who organised emperor worship and could use statues that seemed to speak or move.
symbols.meaning: The religious power that serves the political beast by deception, persuading people to worship it.

readings.reading: Some (Chilton) see the apostate Jewish religious leadership that allied with Rome; others the provincial imperial cult.
The papal hierarchy and clergy as the spiritual arm of the papal system.
A future individual religious leader who promotes the worship of the Antichrist.
False religion and ideology that legitimise oppressive power in every era.

symbols.phrase: Battle on the great day of God the Almighty
symbols.jewish: The day of the LORD is "great" in Joel 2:11, 31 and Zephaniah 1:14. The prophets foresee God gathering the nations for judgment: Joel 3:2, 9-14 (the valley of Jehoshaphat), Zephaniah 3:8, Zechariah 12:3 and 14:2 (all nations against Jerusalem), and Ezekiel 38-39 (Gog). The same gathering reappears in Revelation 19:19 and 20:8, and Psalm 2:2 shows the kings gathered against the LORD and his Anointed.
symbols.meaning: The demonic spirits think they are gathering the kings for their own war, but in fact they bring them to God's day of judgment. Many scholars note that the definite article ("the battle") and the repeated wording connect 16:14, 19:19 and 20:8 as one final battle.

readings.reading: The battles of 16:14, 19:19 and 20:8 are the same final conflict described three times; this supports reading Revelation 20 as recapitulating the church age (Beale, Riddlebarger).
The campaign of Armageddon at the end of the tribulation, ended by Christ's return in 19:11-21; the battle of 20:8 is a separate revolt after the millennium.
The "day" of the Lord's judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70, when Rome and its allies gathered against the city.

symbols.phrase: Behold, I am coming like a thief. Blessed is the one who stays awake and clothed
symbols.jewish: Jesus used the image of the thief for his coming (Matthew 24:43; Luke 12:39), and Paul and Peter echo it (1 Thessalonians 5:2; 2 Peter 3:10). Sardis is warned that Christ will come like a thief (Revelation 3:3) and Laodicea told to buy white garments to cover its nakedness (3:18). The Mishnah (compiled c. 200, later than Revelation) describes the captain of the Temple Mount making night rounds; a Levite found asleep at his post could be beaten and have his clothes burned (Mishnah Middot 1:2).
symbols.cultural: Nakedness and public exposure were deep shame in honour-shame cultures; prisoners and the defeated were stripped.
symbols.meaning: A sudden interruption in the narrative, in Christ's own voice, and the third of Revelation's seven beatitudes. In the middle of the gathering for battle, readers are told to stay alert and keep their garments: faithful lives. It shows that the vision is aimed at the church's present conduct.

readings.reading: Christ's coming in judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70, which Jesus said would come within that generation; Christians were to be ready to flee (Luke 21:20-22).
The Parousia itself, which occurred in AD 70.
The Second Coming at the end of the tribulation; dispensationalists apply the warning to tribulation believers rather than to a church already raptured.
The one Second Coming at the end of the age, for which the church must always be ready.

symbols.phrase: The place called in Hebrew Armageddon
symbols.jewish: Most take Har-Magedon as Hebrew "mountain of Megiddo". Megiddo guarded the pass into the Jezreel valley and was a famous battlefield: Deborah and Barak defeated the kings of Canaan "by the waters of Megiddo" (Judges 5:19); King Josiah fell there (2 Kings 23:29-30; 2 Chronicles 35:22); Zechariah 12:11 speaks of great mourning "in the plain of Megiddo" over one whom they pierced (compare Revelation 1:7). But Megiddo is a mound, not a mountain, and there was no known "mount of Megiddo". Alternatives include "mount of assembly" (har mo'ed, the mountain of the gods in Isaiah 14:13), nearby Mount Carmel (where Elijah defeated the prophets of Baal, 1 Kings 18), or Mount Zion/Jerusalem, where the prophets place the final battle (Joel 3; Zechariah 12; 14; Ezekiel 38-39 on "the mountains of Israel").
symbols.cultural: The Jezreel valley below Megiddo was a corridor for armies from Thutmose III (15th century BC) onward; "in Hebrew" signals a riddle-like name, as with Abaddon (9:11).
symbols.meaning: The name evokes the place where God's enemies are defeated and the world mourns. Whether it is a literal location or a symbolic name for the final battle is disputed; most scholars think John chose a name with rich associations rather than a map reference.

readings.reading: A literal staging area in the valley of Jezreel near Megiddo for a campaign that culminates at Jerusalem when Christ returns (Walvoord; Thomas).
A symbolic name recalling Israel's great defeats and mourning, applied to the armies gathered against Jerusalem in AD 66-70 (Chilton).
The final great conflict between Christ and the coalition of papal, infidel and anti-Christian powers, often linked by its interpreters with events and alliances of their own day.
Not a geographical place but a symbol of the final battle in which the world gathers against the church and is destroyed by Christ; the same event as 19:19-21 and 20:7-10.
Beale and others read it as a symbolic "Megiddo-mountain" that blends Megiddo with the mountains of Israel of Ezekiel 38-39, describing the last attack on God's people.

symbols.phrase: The seventh angel poured out his bowl into the air
symbols.jewish: Satan is called "the ruler of the power of the air" in Ephesians 2:2; Jewish cosmology placed evil spirits in the lower heavens (2 Enoch; Testament of Benjamin 3:4). The air is also the source of the storm that follows (lightning, thunder, hail).
symbols.cultural: Greek physics counted air as one of the four elements; after earth, sea, waters and sun, the air completes the elements struck.
symbols.meaning: The last bowl reaches the whole environment of human life and, for many interpreters, the realm of the demonic powers. It produces the final storm and earthquake.

symbols.phrase: A loud voice from the throne: It is done!
symbols.jewish: The Greek gegonen recalls Ezekiel 39:8 ("it is coming and it shall be done") about the defeat of Gog. It anticipates Revelation 21:6 ("It is done") at the new creation, and resembles Jesus' cry "It is finished" (John 19:30), though the verb differs.
symbols.meaning: God's judgment on evil is complete. The voice from the throne in the temple shows it is God's own declaration.

readings.reading: The end of the old covenant order with the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70.
The completion of God's wrath at the very end of the tribulation, just before Christ returns.
The final judgment that ends history, seen from the perspective of the seventh and last bowl.

symbols.phrase: A great earthquake such as had never occurred since men were on the earth
symbols.jewish: Lightning, rumblings and thunder recall God's appearance at Sinai (Exodus 19:16-19) and grow in intensity through Revelation (4:5; 8:5; 11:19; 16:18). The prophets foresee God shaking heaven and earth (Haggai 2:6; Hebrews 12:26-27) and a great earthquake in the land in the battle with Gog (Ezekiel 38:19-20; Zechariah 14:4-5). "Such as had never been" echoes Daniel 12:1 and Exodus 9:18, 24.
symbols.cultural: Asia Minor was prone to earthquakes. Tacitus records the AD 17 earthquake that destroyed twelve cities in one night, including Sardis and Philadelphia (Annals 2.47), and Laodicea was destroyed in AD 60.
symbols.meaning: The climax of God's appearing in judgment: the whole structure of human society is shaken. Many see the language of cosmic shaking as covenantal imagery for the end of an order (as in Haggai 2:6); others as literal and final.

readings.reading: Covenantal "decreation" language for the end of the Jewish order in AD 70, interpreted through Hebrews 12:26-28, where the shaking removes the old so the unshakable kingdom remains.
A literal, unprecedented global earthquake at the end of the tribulation (Zechariah 14:4).
The final shaking of creation at the last judgment.

symbols.phrase: The great city split into three parts; the cities of the nations collapsed
symbols.jewish: In Ezekiel 5:1-12 the prophet divides his shaved hair into three parts as a sign of Jerusalem's fate: a third burned in the city, a third struck by the sword, a third scattered. Zechariah 14:4 sees the Mount of Olives split by an earthquake. "The great city" is Jerusalem in Revelation 11:8 ("where their Lord was crucified") and Babylon in 14:8, 17:18 and 18:10-21.
symbols.cultural: Josephus describes Jerusalem during the siege as split into three warring factions under John of Gischala, Simon bar Giora and Eleazar (Jewish War 5.1-4). Rome in AD 69 was torn by civil war.
symbols.meaning: The great city is utterly broken, and with it the cities of the nations that shared its life. The identity of "the great city" is central to the debate about Babylon.

readings.reading: The great city is Jerusalem (as in 11:8), divided into three factions during the siege and destroyed in AD 70; the Ezekiel 5 pattern confirms it (Chilton, Gentry).
Papal Rome and the political-religious system it headed, broken up in the final judgment; the "cities of the nations" are the kingdoms of Christendom.
Either a literal end-time Babylon or Jerusalem split by a literal earthquake (Zechariah 14:4); Walvoord takes the great city as Babylon, distinct from the cities of the nations.
The great city is the world city of every age, human society organised against God, which collapses at the end.

symbols.phrase: God remembered Babylon the great and gave her the cup of the wine of the fury of His wrath
symbols.jewish: The cup of God's wrath is a stock prophetic image: Psalm 75:8; Isaiah 51:17, 22 (Jerusalem drinks it); Jeremiah 25:15-29 (the nations, Babylon last); Jeremiah 51:7 (Babylon a golden cup in the LORD's hand). The Qumran Habakkuk commentary says the Wicked Priest will drink the cup of the LORD's wrath (1QpHab 11:10-15). "God remembered" is covenant language (Genesis 8:1; Exodus 2:24) here used for judgment (Psalm 137:7).
symbols.cultural: Wine was mixed with water in Greek and Roman custom; "unmixed" wine (14:10) was strong and intoxicating. Babylon's own cup of seduction (17:4; 18:6) is turned back on her.
symbols.meaning: God has not forgotten the city's crimes; she must drink the full cup she made others drink. The verse previews chapters 17-18, which expand the fall of Babylon.

symbols.phrase: Every island fled and no mountain could be found
symbols.jewish: Compare the sixth seal (Revelation 6:14) and the great white throne (20:11). Mountains melt and flee at God's coming (Judges 5:5; Psalm 97:5; Nahum 1:5; Isaiah 40:4; 1 Enoch 1:6).
symbols.meaning: The stable features of creation give way before God's presence. Interpreters differ whether this is literal geological upheaval or the prophetic language of theophany used for the fall of world orders.

readings.reading: Prophetic theophany imagery (as in Isaiah 13 for Babylon or Isaiah 34 for Edom) for the collapse of a nation, here Israel and its world in AD 70.
Literal topographical changes at Christ's return.
The dissolution of the present order at the final judgment (20:11).

symbols.phrase: Great hailstones weighing about a hundred pounds
symbols.jewish: The seventh Egyptian plague was hail with fire (Exodus 9:22-26); God threw hailstones on the Amorites (Joshua 10:11) and will rain hail on Gog (Ezekiel 38:22); hail is in God's storehouse for the day of battle (Job 38:22-23; Isaiah 28:2, 17). The penalty for blasphemy in the law was stoning (Leviticus 24:16), and here those who blaspheme are stoned from heaven.
symbols.cultural: The Greek talantiaia means "the weight of a talent", roughly 20 to 45 kg depending on the standard. Josephus says the Roman siege engines at Jerusalem threw white stones weighing a talent, and that watchmen shouted a warning as each one came (Jewish War 5.269-273).
symbols.meaning: The final, crushing blow of judgment from heaven, yet the survivors still curse God.

readings.reading: Chilton and others point to Josephus' talent-weight stones hurled by Roman catapults into Jerusalem in AD 70: the covenant penalty of stoning for blasphemy inflicted on the city.
Literal, enormous hail falling at the end of the tribulation.
A symbol of overwhelming final judgment, modelled on the Egyptian plague of hail.

The bowls are the covenant judgments on Jerusalem and the land culminating in AD 70. Sores recall the Deuteronomy 28 curses; the sea and rivers of blood recall the massacres Josephus describes; the Euphrates opens for Rome's eastern legions and client kings; Armageddon symbolises the gathering of armies against Jerusalem; the great city split in three is Jerusalem divided into factions and destroyed; the talent-weight hail matches the Roman catapult stones (Chilton, Gentry). Some preterists who identify Babylon with Rome read the fifth bowl as Rome's civil war of AD 68-69.

Agrees with the partial preterist mapping onto AD 66-70 but holds that "It is done" marks the full end of redemptive history, the Parousia and the judgment of the dead, all fulfilled in AD 70 (King, Preston). Critics, including partial preterists, say this collapses the final resurrection and Second Coming into a past event in a way the historic creeds deny; proponents answer that the New Testament time statements require it.

The bowls fall from the French Revolution onward: the ulcer of revolutionary infidelity (first), the naval wars (second), the river campaigns in persecuting lands (third), the Napoleonic wars (fourth), the humbling of the papal throne in 1798-1809 (fifth), the drying of Ottoman power (sixth), and a still-future final judgment (seventh) (Elliott, Barnes).

The bowls are literal, worldwide plagues in the last part of the future tribulation. The Euphrates will be dried for eastern armies; demonic spirits will gather the nations to the valley of Megiddo; Christ will return to defeat them; a literal earthquake will split Jerusalem or end-time Babylon and level the cities of the world (Walvoord, Thomas). Dispensationalists see the church already raptured; historic premillennialists (Ladd) see the church present and protected through these judgments.

The bowls portray God's judgments on the impenitent in every age, culminating in the last judgment. Armageddon is not a place on a map but the final attack of the world on the church, the same battle as 19:19 and 20:8. The constant refrain "they did not repent" exposes the hardening of human hearts (Hendriksen, Milligan).

Beale reads the bowls as covering the period between Christ's first and second comings while culminating in the end, with Armageddon as a symbolic name for the final battle that recapitulates 19:19-21 and 20:7-10. Osborne leans futurist while stressing the symbolic use of Exodus imagery.
The repeated description of a single final battle (16:14; 19:19; 20:8) supports reading Revelation 20 as a recapitulation of the church age rather than a sequel to chapter 19.

Armageddon is the climactic campaign of the seven-year tribulation, after which Christ sets up a literal thousand-year reign in Jerusalem; the Gog and Magog revolt of 20:8 is a separate event after the millennium.

questions: Why do the bowls follow the order of the trumpets (earth, sea, rivers, sun) while being total rather than partial? What does this suggest about the structure of Revelation?
The angel of the waters and the altar both declare God's judgments just. How does the "blood for blood" principle (16:6) fit with the Lamb who conquers by his own blood?
Is Armageddon a place, a symbol or both? What do the associations of Megiddo (Judges 5, 2 Kings 23, Zechariah 12) add to the image?
Why does Christ's beatitude about watchfulness (16:15) interrupt the gathering for battle?
Who is "the great city" of 16:19: Jerusalem (11:8), Rome, a future city or the world system? What clues in the text point each way?

title: The Great Prostitute on the Scarlet Beast
summary: One of the bowl angels shows John the judgment of the great prostitute who sits on many waters, with whom the kings of the earth committed immorality. In a wilderness he sees a woman dressed in purple and scarlet, glittering with gold and pearls, holding a golden cup of abominations and riding a scarlet beast with seven heads and ten horns. Her forehead bears the name "Babylon the great, mother of prostitutes", and she is drunk with the blood of the saints. The angel explains the mystery: the beast "was, and is not, and is about to come up from the abyss"; its seven heads are seven mountains and seven kings, five fallen, one present and one still to come, and the beast itself is an eighth; its ten horns are ten kings who rule with it for one hour and make war on the Lamb, who conquers them. Finally the beast and the ten horns turn on the prostitute, strip her, devour her flesh and burn her, because God put it into their hearts; the woman is "the great city that rules over the kings of the earth".

outline.heading: Invitation: the judgment of the great prostitute
The vision: the woman on the scarlet beast, her dress, cup, name and drunkenness
The mystery of the beast that was, is not and will come
Seven heads: seven mountains and seven kings; the eighth
Ten horns: ten kings who war against the Lamb and lose
The waters explained; the beast destroys the prostitute; the woman is the great city

context:
The chapter is a portrait of a city as a prostitute, a standard prophetic image. Isaiah calls Jerusalem a harlot (Isaiah 1:21); Jeremiah 2-3 and Ezekiel 16 and 23 develop at length the picture of Jerusalem and Samaria as adulterous women; Hosea applies it to Israel. But pagan cities are also harlots: Tyre is a forgotten prostitute singing for her trade (Isaiah 23:15-18) and Nineveh is the "mistress of sorceries" who seduced nations (Nahum 3:4). Babylon itself is the city that "dwells on many waters" (Jeremiah 51:13), a golden cup in the LORD's hand that made the nations drunk (Jeremiah 51:7), a queen who says she will never be a widow (Isaiah 47:7-8). After AD 70, Jewish writings used "Babylon" as a code name for Rome, which like Nebuchadnezzar had destroyed the temple (4 Ezra 3:1-2, 28-31; 2 Baruch 10:1-3; 11:1; 67:7; Sibylline Oracles 5.143, 159), and 1 Peter 5:13 uses Babylon for the city where Peter writes, usually taken as Rome. The beast and its heads and horns come from Daniel 7, where the fourth beast has ten horns and a little horn that blasphemes and wars against the saints.

The Roman setting is vivid. Rome was famous as the city on seven hills (Virgil, Georgics 2.535; Horace, Carmen Saeculare 7; Martial 4.64; Cicero, Letters to Atticus 6.5), celebrated annually in the Septimontium festival. A sestertius of Vespasian (AD 71) shows the goddess Roma seated on the seven hills with the river Tiber at her feet, a remarkable parallel to a woman seated on seven mountains by many waters. The goddess Roma was worshipped in temples across Asia Minor, often alongside the emperor. The "was, is not, will come" riddle evokes the Nero redivivus legend, the rumour that Nero had not truly died (or would rise) and would return from the east (Tacitus, Histories 2.8-9; Suetonius, Nero 57; Dio Cassius 64.9). The identity of Babylon is one of the great disputes of Revelation study: first-century Rome; first-century Jerusalem; papal Rome; a future rebuilt Babylon or end-time world capital; or the world system in every age. The arguments are summarised in the readings below, and each view is held by careful scholars.

symbols.phrase: The great prostitute
symbols.jewish: In the prophets a city that forsakes God or trades with the nations for gain is a prostitute: Jerusalem (Isaiah 1:21; Jeremiah 3:1-10; Ezekiel 16; 23), Samaria (Ezekiel 23), Israel (Hosea 2), Tyre (Isaiah 23:15-18) and Nineveh (Nahum 3:4). The image stands in deliberate contrast to the Bride, the New Jerusalem, introduced with the same formula ("one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls came and said, Come, I will show you", 17:1; 21:9).
symbols.cultural: Prostitution was legal and widespread in Roman cities; brothels and courtesans were part of urban life. "Fornication" was also a familiar metaphor for idolatry and for commercial and political compromise.
symbols.meaning: The prostitute is a city whose power over the nations rests on seduction: idolatry, economic exploitation and political alliance. The parallel with the Bride invites a "tale of two cities", the city of man and the city of God.

readings.reading: Gentry and Chilton argue that "harlot" is the Old Testament's main word for unfaithful Jerusalem (Ezekiel 16; 23) and implies a covenant partner who has broken faith, which a pagan city never was.
The seductive world system of every age that draws people away from God by luxury, power and false religion (Hendriksen).
The apostate church of Rome, unfaithful to Christ her husband (Reformers, Elliott, Barnes).
Walvoord identifies her with a future apostate world religion, which the Antichrist first uses and then destroys.

symbols.phrase: Who sits on many waters
symbols.jewish: Jeremiah 51:13 addresses Babylon as the one who dwells by many waters, referring to the Euphrates and its canals. Waters are peoples in Isaiah 8:7 and 17:12-13. Revelation 17:15 explains them as "peoples, multitudes, nations and tongues", the fourfold formula used throughout the book (5:9; 7:9; 13:7).
symbols.cultural: Rome's empire was built on Mediterranean sea power; the Vespasian coin of Roma on seven hills shows the Tiber at her feet.
symbols.meaning: The prostitute rules over and depends on the peoples of the world. The image is borrowed from the literal geography of ancient Babylon and given an international meaning.

readings.reading: Gentry answers the objection that Jerusalem did not rule nations: the waters represent Jerusalem's influence over the Jewish diaspora throughout the empire and her political standing with Rome.
The worldwide extent of the end-time religious-political system.
The universal reach of worldly seduction.

symbols.phrase: The kings of the earth were immoral with her; earth-dwellers drunk with the wine of her immorality
symbols.jewish: Tyre "commits prostitution with all the kingdoms" by trade (Isaiah 23:17); Babylon made the nations drunk with her wine (Jeremiah 51:7). "Those who dwell on the earth" is a stock phrase in Revelation for unbelieving humanity (3:10; 6:10; 13:8).
symbols.cultural: Client kings and allied cities gained wealth and status by honouring Rome and the emperor, often through temples and festivals of the imperial cult; this was the "intoxicating" benefit of the Pax Romana.
symbols.meaning: Immorality here is mainly a metaphor for idolatrous and economic alliance with the city, though literal vice may be included. Many interpreters (Bauckham, Koester) stress the economic dimension that chapter 18 develops.

readings.reading: Some preterists read "kings of the earth" as "kings of the land": the Herodian rulers and Jerusalem's leaders who allied with Rome (Chilton).
World leaders who join the end-time religious and economic system.

symbols.phrase: Carried away in the Spirit into a wilderness
symbols.jewish: Ezekiel is repeatedly carried by the Spirit to see visions (Ezekiel 3:12-14; 8:3; 11:24; 43:5). Isaiah 21:1-10 is an oracle about "the wilderness of the sea", ending "Fallen, fallen is Babylon". The phrase "in the Spirit" marks major visions in Revelation (1:10; 4:2; 17:3; 21:10).
symbols.meaning: The wilderness setting draws on Isaiah 21 and contrasts with the "great, high mountain" from which John sees the New Jerusalem (21:10). It may also contrast with the woman of chapter 12, who is protected in the wilderness, whereas this woman will be left desolate (17:16).

symbols.phrase: A scarlet beast with seven heads and ten horns
symbols.jewish: The beast is the sea beast of Revelation 13:1, which combines the four beasts of Daniel 7 and resembles the red dragon of 12:3. The ten horns come from Daniel's fourth beast (Daniel 7:7, 24).
symbols.cultural: Scarlet dye (from the kermes insect) was costly and associated with military commanders' cloaks and with royalty and wealth.
symbols.meaning: The woman rides the beast: she is carried and supported by the political-military power, but the arrangement is unstable, as 17:16 shows. Most interpreters see the beast as an imperial power (in John's day, Rome).

readings.reading: The beast is Rome (and Nero); the harlot riding it is Jerusalem, allied with and dependent on Rome against Christ and the church (Gentry). Preterists who identify Babylon with Rome instead see the city and its empire.
The Roman empire in its later, papal-supported form; the harlot (papal church) riding the secular powers of Europe (Barnes, Elliott).
The Antichrist and his revived Roman or world empire, supporting an apostate religious system (Walvoord).
Persecuting political power in every age, with seductive worldly culture riding on its back.

symbols.phrase: Covered with blasphemous names
symbols.jewish: The little horn speaks great things against the Most High (Daniel 7:8, 25; 11:36); the sea beast has blasphemous names on its heads (Revelation 13:1, 5-6).
symbols.cultural: Emperors bore divine titles on coins and inscriptions: divi filius (son of the deified one), Augustus (revered, sebastos), pontifex maximus, soter (saviour), kyrios (lord), and in some cities theos (god). Domitian reportedly encouraged "lord and god" (Suetonius, Domitian 13).
symbols.meaning: The beast claims for itself titles that belong to God alone. For first-century readers, imperial titles on coins in their purses were the obvious example.

readings.reading: Papal titles such as "Vicar of Christ", "Holy Father" and claims of universal headship were seen by historicists as blasphemous names.
The future Antichrist will claim divinity (2 Thessalonians 2:4).

symbols.phrase: Dressed in purple and scarlet, adorned with gold, precious stones and pearls
symbols.jewish: Purple, scarlet, gold and gems were materials of the tabernacle and the high priest's garments (Exodus 25:4; 28:5-8, 15-21). Jeremiah 4:30 pictures Jerusalem dressing in scarlet and gold to attract lovers who will kill her; Ezekiel 16:10-18 describes Jerusalem using God's gifts of fine clothing and jewels for her prostitution. The king of Tyre is covered with precious stones (Ezekiel 28:13).
symbols.cultural: Tyrian purple was the most expensive dye in the Roman world, reserved by law and custom for magistrates, senators and emperors; pearls were the supreme luxury (Pliny, Natural History 9.106-123). Courtesans displayed such finery.
symbols.meaning: Wealth, royalty and seductive luxury. The same list of colours and materials returns in the merchants' cargo (18:12) and their lament (18:16), and contrasts with the Bride, dressed in pure linen (19:8), and the New Jerusalem built of gold and jewels (21:18-21).

readings.reading: Gentry and Chilton read the colours as priestly and tabernacle colours (Exodus 28), pointing to Jerusalem and its priesthood corrupted into harlotry.
The scarlet and purple of cardinals and bishops and the wealth of the papal court were cited by Reformers and later historicists.
The wealth and splendour of the end-time religious and commercial system.
The alluring wealth and pomp of worldly power in every era.

symbols.phrase: A golden cup full of abominations and the impurities of her immorality
symbols.jewish: Babylon was "a golden cup in the LORD's hand, making all the earth drunk" (Jeremiah 51:7). "Abomination" (Hebrew to'evah, shiqquts) is the Old Testament term for idols and idolatrous practices (Deuteronomy 29:17; 1 Kings 11:5-7) and appears in Daniel's "abomination of desolation" (Daniel 9:27; 11:31; 12:11).
symbols.cultural: A golden drinking vessel spoke of extravagant banquets; libation bowls were used in pagan cult.
symbols.meaning: Outwardly splendid, inwardly corrupt: the cup offers luxury and belonging but contains idolatry and moral filth. Her cup is answered by the cup of God's wrath (16:19; 18:6).

readings.reading: Some preterists connect the cup with the temple vessels and the "abomination" language of Daniel and Matthew 24:15, applied to Jerusalem's corrupt worship.
Protestant interpreters connected the cup with the Mass chalice and the doctrines they regarded as corruptions.

symbols.phrase: On her forehead a name was written, a mystery
symbols.jewish: Jeremiah 3:3 speaks of Judah having "a prostitute's forehead" and refusing to blush. The high priest wore a golden plate on his forehead inscribed "Holy to the LORD" (Exodus 28:36-38). God's servants bear his name on their foreheads (Revelation 7:3; 14:1; 22:4), while the beast's followers bear its mark (13:16).
symbols.cultural: Some Roman writers mention prostitutes displaying their names publicly; Seneca refers to a name hanging over a prostitute's brow (Controversiae 1.2.7) and Juvenal describes Messalina using an assumed name in a brothel (Satires 6.122-123). How widely this applied is uncertain.
symbols.meaning: "Mystery" (Greek mysterion) may be part of the name or a note that the name is symbolic and must be interpreted (compare 17:7). The forehead name exposes her true identity.

readings.reading: A deliberate parody of the high priest's forehead plate: instead of "Holy to the LORD" the city bears "Babylon" (Chilton).
Some Protestant writers claimed that "Mysterium" had been inscribed on papal tiaras; this claim is disputed and poorly attested.

symbols.phrase: Babylon the Great
symbols.jewish: Historical Babylon was the empire that destroyed Jerusalem and the first temple (586 BC) and the archetype of proud, idolatrous world power (Genesis 11:1-9; Isaiah 13-14; 47; Jeremiah 50-51; Daniel 4:30, "Is this not great Babylon that I have built?"). After AD 70 Jewish apocalypses use "Babylon" as a code name for Rome, the second destroyer of the temple (4 Ezra 3:1-2, 28-31; 2 Baruch 11:1; 67:7; Sibylline Oracles 5.143, 159); 1 Peter 5:13 uses it for the city where Peter wrote. Jerusalem in turn is called "Sodom" and "Egypt" in Revelation 11:8 and treated as an apostate city in the prophets.
symbols.cultural: Rome was the dominant world city, centre of trade, empire and the imperial cult, built on seven hills; ancient Babylon was largely deserted by the first century (Strabo 16.1.5; Pliny, Natural History 6.122).
symbols.meaning: The identity of Babylon is disputed. Most critical and many evangelical scholars hold that in John's day Babylon was Rome, while noting that the image applies more broadly. Others hold it is Jerusalem, papal Rome, a future city, or the world system as such. Each reading appeals to different features of chapters 17-18.

readings.reading: Jerusalem (Gentry, Chilton, DeMar): "the great city" is where the Lord was crucified (11:8); the harlot image fits a covenant-breaking people; her priestly colours; she is drunk with the blood of prophets and saints, which Jesus laid at Jerusalem's door (Matthew 23:35-37; Luke 13:33); she rides (allies with) the beast Rome and is destroyed by it in AD 70; and she contrasts with the New Jerusalem. Other preterists identify Babylon with Rome and link its fall to the turmoil of AD 68-69 or to Rome's later judgment.

Papal Rome (the Reformers, Westminster-era Puritans, Newton, Elliott, Barnes): the city on seven hills that ruled the kings of Europe, whose church was seen as fallen into spiritual adultery and drunk with the blood of the martyrs of the Inquisition and the Reformation.

A future entity. Some read a literal rebuilt Babylon on the Euphrates in Iraq (Dyer, Woods, Thomas) on the ground that Isaiah 13 and Jeremiah 50-51 were never fully fulfilled; others (Walvoord) see an apostate world religion in chapter 17 and a commercial-political capital in chapter 18, possibly a revived Rome.

The world system of every age, human society organised in pride, luxury and idolatry against God; Rome was its form in John's day but Babylon reappears in every empire and culture (Hendriksen, Beale in part).

Rome in the first instance (the seven hills, the dominant world city, the code name in Jewish writings), and through Rome the recurring pattern of godless civilisation that will reach a final form before Christ returns (Beale, Osborne, Bauckham, Koester).

symbols.phrase: The mother of prostitutes and of the abominations of the earth
symbols.jewish: "Like mother, like daughter" is said of Jerusalem in Ezekiel 16:44-45. Babylon at Babel is the origin of human pride against God (Genesis 11).
symbols.cultural: Rome was hailed as mother of cities and of nations (Roma as mater); colonies were her "daughters".
symbols.meaning: She is the source and prototype of idolatry and corruption, spreading them to others. The title parodies honorific civic titles.

readings.reading: The Church of Rome as "mother church" whose daughters share her errors; some later historicists extended "daughters" to state churches that retained Roman practices.
Jerusalem as the mother city of Judaism, whose apostasy was the root of persecution of the church (Chilton).

symbols.phrase: Drunk with the blood of the saints and witnesses of Jesus
symbols.jewish: Jesus said that all the righteous blood shed on earth would come on Jerusalem and on "this generation" (Matthew 23:35-37) and that a prophet could not perish outside Jerusalem (Luke 13:33). Isaiah 34:5-7 speaks of a sword drunk with blood; oppressors drunk on their own blood (Isaiah 49:26). Revelation 18:24 echoes the charge.
symbols.cultural: Nero's persecution in Rome after the fire of AD 64 killed a great multitude of Christians (Tacitus, Annals 15.44; 1 Clement 5-6), including, by tradition, Peter and Paul. Local persecutions in Asia (Antipas at Pergamum, Revelation 2:13) also form the background.
symbols.meaning: The city delights in the deaths of the faithful as a drunkard delights in wine. John's "great amazement" (17:6) is perhaps because she appears so attractive.

readings.reading: Jerusalem: from Stephen (Acts 7) to James (Acts 12; Josephus, Antiquities 20.200), Jerusalem's leaders persecuted the church, and Jesus explicitly laid the blood of the prophets at Jerusalem's door (Gentry).
Papal Rome, held responsible for the deaths of Waldensians, Albigensians, Lollards, Hussites and Protestants.
The end-time religious system that persecutes tribulation believers.
Rome under Nero and later emperors, and every power that persecutes Christians.

symbols.phrase: The beast that was, and is not, and is about to come up out of the Abyss
keywords: is not, and yet will be
symbols.jewish: It is a parody of God's name, "who is and who was and who is to come" (Revelation 1:4, 8; 4:8), and of the Lamb who was dead and lives (1:18; 2:8). The beast's "fatal wound that was healed" (13:3, 12, 14) is the same idea. The abyss is the prison of demonic powers (9:1-11; 11:7; 20:1-3; compare 1 Enoch 10:4-6; 18:11-16).
symbols.cultural: After Nero's suicide in AD 68 many believed he was alive or would return; several pretenders appeared in the east (Tacitus, Histories 2.8-9; Suetonius, Nero 57; Dio Cassius 64.9; 66.19). Jewish and Christian Sibylline Oracles turned him into a returning eschatological enemy (Sibylline Oracles 4.119-139; 5.137-154, 361-385; later Ascension of Isaiah 4:2-4).
symbols.meaning: The beast imitates resurrection: it appears to die and returns from the abyss, but its destiny is destruction (Greek apoleia, 17:8, 11). Many scholars think John uses the Nero legend; others think the "death and return" refers to the empire rather than a person.

readings.reading: The Roman empire "died" in the chaos of AD 68-69 after Nero's death and "revived" under Vespasian (Gentry); the beast was Nero as head of Rome.
Pagan imperial Rome that fell (AD 476) and revived as the papal and Holy Roman power.
The future Antichrist, who may suffer an apparent death and revival, or the Roman empire that ceased and will be revived in the last days (Walvoord).
Persecuting power in every age seems to be defeated and then reappears in new forms, until its final destruction.
John uses the Nero redivivus legend as a symbol: the persecuting emperor returns in Domitian or in a future Nero-like figure (Bauckham, Aune, Koester).

symbols.phrase: Whose names were not written in the Book of Life from the foundation of the world
symbols.jewish: God keeps a book of the living (Exodus 32:32-33; Psalm 69:28; Isaiah 4:3; Daniel 12:1; Malachi 3:16). Jewish texts speak of heavenly books recording the righteous and the deeds of all (1 Enoch 47:3; 108:3; Jubilees 30:20-22). Revelation 13:8 calls it "the book of life of the Lamb who was slain".
symbols.cultural: Greek cities kept citizen registers, and a condemned citizen's name could be erased.
symbols.meaning: The faithful are secure because God enrolled them from the beginning; the world "marvels" at the beast because it has no anchor in God. The phrase raises questions of predestination that interpreters answer differently.

symbols.phrase: This calls for a mind with wisdom
symbols.jewish: The same call to wisdom introduces the number of the beast (Revelation 13:18). Daniel says the wise will understand (Daniel 12:10); the maskilim (wise teachers) of Daniel 11:33-35 instruct the people under persecution.
symbols.meaning: The reader is invited to decode the symbol. The decoding is itself symbolic and layered: the heads are both mountains and kings. Interpreters agree that John signals a puzzle, not on how to solve it.

symbols.phrase: The seven heads are seven mountains on which the woman sits
symbols.jewish: In the prophets mountains can symbolise kingdoms: the stone becomes a mountain filling the earth (Daniel 2:35, 44-45); Babylon is a "destroying mountain" (Jeremiah 51:25); the mountain of the LORD's house (Isaiah 2:2). Jerusalem was built on hills (Psalm 125:2), and some later Jewish texts count seven, though this is late and uncertain.
symbols.cultural: Rome was proverbially "the city of seven hills" (Palatine, Capitoline, Quirinal, Viminal, Esquiline, Caelian, Aventine), a commonplace in Latin poets (Virgil, Georgics 2.535; Horace, Carmen Saeculare 7; Propertius 3.11.57; Martial 4.64) and celebrated in the Septimontium. A sestertius of Vespasian (AD 71) shows Roma seated on seven hills.
symbols.meaning: For most interpreters this is the clearest pointer to Rome in the chapter. The "mountains" are immediately explained also as kings, so the image may be political rather than topographical.

readings.reading: Gentry agrees the seven mountains are Rome, but notes they belong to the beast, not the woman: the harlot (Jerusalem) "sits" on Rome in the sense of being allied with and supported by it.
Rome, seat of the papacy, confirming the identification of Babylon with papal Rome (Barnes, Elliott).
Many futurists read mountains as kingdoms (Daniel 2): seven world empires through history (Walvoord); others accept a reference to Rome and expect a revived Rome.
The completeness of worldly power on which the seductive world culture rests.
A deliberate reference to Rome that also symbolises the fullness of political power (Beale, Bauckham).

symbols.phrase: Seven kings: five have fallen, one is, the other has not yet come
symbols.jewish: Daniel 7:17 explains beasts as kings, and Daniel 8 and 11 list successive rulers. The number seven may be literal or symbolic of completeness.
symbols.cultural: Lists of Roman emperors differ on where to start (Julius Caesar or Augustus) and whether to count the brief rulers of AD 68-69 (Galba, Otho, Vitellius). Ancient writers such as Suetonius (The Twelve Caesars) and the Sibylline Oracles (5.12-51) began with Julius; Tacitus (Annals 1.1) begins the principate with Augustus.
symbols.meaning: The verse is a key text for dating Revelation, and it is disputed. If "one is" can be identified, it dates the book. But many scholars think the seven are symbolic, meaning the series of rulers is nearly complete and the end is near.

readings.reading: Counting from Julius Caesar: Julius, Augustus, Tiberius, Gaius (Caligula) and Claudius have fallen; Nero "is"; Galba, who reigned only seven months, is the one who "remains a little while". This supports a date before AD 68 (Gentry, Before Jerusalem Fell).

Late-date scholars either count from Augustus and skip the three brief rulers, making Vespasian the one who "is" and Titus the short-lived seventh, with Domitian as the eighth (Nero returned in spirit); or regard the seven as symbolic of the whole series of emperors (Bauckham, Aune, Beale, Koester).

Seven forms of Roman government listed by Livy and Tacitus (kings, consuls, decemvirs, dictators, military tribunes, emperors, and a seventh short-lived form), with the papacy as the eighth (Barnes, Elliott).
Seven successive world empires: Egypt, Assyria, Babylon, Persia, Greece (fallen), Rome (is), and a future kingdom, with the Antichrist's empire as the eighth (Walvoord and others).
Seven is the number of completeness; the kings stand for the whole sequence of world powers that oppose God, and the end is always near (Hendriksen).

symbols.phrase: The beast is an eighth king, who belongs to the seven and goes to destruction
symbols.jewish: Daniel's little horn arises after the ten and is different from them (Daniel 7:8, 24). Early Christian numerology saw eight as the number of resurrection (the eighth day, Sunday), and the beast parodies Christ's resurrection.
symbols.cultural: The Nero redivivus legend pictured Nero returning as a new ruler after the others. Bauckham notes that Neron Kaisar in Hebrew letters sums to 666 and that 888 was used by some early Christians for the name of Jesus in Greek, so "eighth" may be part of a parody.
symbols.meaning: The beast is one of the seven returning as an eighth: an evil ruler revived. Its destiny is destruction.

readings.reading: Either Vespasian as the revival of the empire after Nero, or Rome itself as the beast that sums up the seven heads (Gentry).
The papacy, which inherited the power of imperial Rome while being a new form.
