The future Antichrist, either a revived ruler from history or one who rules after a seventh world empire (Walvoord).
A Nero-like emperor (Domitian for many late-date scholars) or a final Antichrist figure modelled on Nero (Bauckham, Aune).
The persistent spirit of antichristian power, which always "belongs to" the earlier powers and always heads for ruin.

symbols.phrase: The ten horns are ten kings who have not yet received a kingdom
symbols.jewish: Daniel 7:7-8, 20, 24: the fourth beast has ten horns, ten kings who arise from that kingdom. "Horn" symbolises power (Psalm 75:10; Zechariah 1:18-21).
symbols.cultural: Rome ruled through provincial governors and client kings. The Nero legend in the Sibylline Oracles pictured him returning with eastern (Parthian) kings to destroy Rome.
symbols.meaning: Subordinate rulers who give their power to the beast for a short time and join it in opposing the Lamb. Ten probably signals completeness of earthly powers rather than an exact count, though futurists often take it literally.

readings.reading: Rulers of the Roman provinces or client kings who joined Rome against Jerusalem in AD 66-70 (Chilton, Gentry).
The ten Germanic kingdoms that arose from the break-up of the western Roman empire (Vandals, Ostrogoths, Franks, and others), which supported the papacy (Elliott, Barnes, Newton).
A future ten-nation confederacy, often a revived Roman empire in Europe or the Mediterranean, that hands power to the Antichrist (Walvoord).
All the powers of the earth that ally with antichristian authority in every age.
Allies of a returning Nero-like emperor (eastern kings), used symbolically for all rulers who support the beast (Bauckham, Aune).

symbols.phrase: One hour of authority as kings, along with the beast
symbols.jewish: Daniel 4:19 (Greek text) uses "one hour" for a short time; the prophets use "hour" for the appointed time of judgment. "One hour" recurs for Babylon's sudden fall (18:10, 17, 19).
symbols.meaning: A very short period of power: the alliance against the Lamb is brief and doomed.

symbols.phrase: The Lamb will triumph, because He is Lord of lords and King of kings
symbols.jewish: Deuteronomy 10:17 ("God of gods and Lord of lords"); Psalm 136:2-3; the Greek of Daniel 4:37 calls God "God of gods, Lord of lords and King of kings". 1 Enoch 9:4 and 2 Maccabees 13:4 use similar titles. "King of kings" was the title of Babylonian and Persian monarchs (Ezekiel 26:7; Ezra 7:12; Daniel 2:37).
symbols.cultural: Parthian rulers used "king of kings" on their coins; Roman emperors were acclaimed lords. The Lamb outranks them all.
symbols.meaning: Divine titles given to the Lamb. The title is reversed in 19:16 (King of kings and Lord of lords). The war is won by the Lamb, whose weapon is his sacrificial death and his word (19:15).

symbols.phrase: Those with Him are called and chosen and faithful
symbols.jewish: "Many are called but few are chosen" (Matthew 22:14). Israel was God's chosen people (Deuteronomy 7:6); the War Scroll at Qumran describes the "chosen ones" fighting in the final war of the sons of light (1QM 12:1-5).
symbols.meaning: The Lamb's companions share his victory. Unlike the War Scroll, Revelation's saints conquer by faithfulness and witness, not by arms (12:11).

readings.reading: The armies of heaven, including the glorified church, returning with Christ (19:14).
All faithful believers who share Christ's victory throughout history.

symbols.phrase: The ten horns and the beast will hate the prostitute, make her desolate and naked, eat her flesh and burn her with fire
symbols.jewish: Ezekiel 16:37-41 and 23:25-29 describe Jerusalem's lovers turning on her, stripping her naked and burning her houses; Jeremiah 4:30 says her lovers will seek her life. Eating flesh recalls Jezebel devoured by dogs (2 Kings 9:36) and Micah 3:3. Leviticus 21:9 decrees that a priest's daughter who prostitutes herself must be burned with fire.
symbols.cultural: Rome was burned in the great fire of AD 64; the Capitol was burned during the civil war in December 69. The Nero legend in the Sibylline Oracles imagined Nero returning to burn Rome.
symbols.meaning: Evil is self-destructive: the political power that carried the seductive city turns against her. This is one of the most important verses for the identity debate, because the city is destroyed by the beast itself.

readings.reading: Rome (the beast) and its allies destroyed Jerusalem (the harlot) in AD 70, burning the city and temple; the Ezekiel 16 and 23 background and the priestly burning law (Leviticus 21:9) fit Jerusalem precisely (Gentry, Chilton).
The nations of Europe turning on the papacy: the Reformation, the French Revolution's confiscation of church property, and the loss of the Papal States (1870).
The Antichrist and his ten kings will destroy the apostate world church (ecclesiastical Babylon) at mid-tribulation to demand worship for himself (Walvoord).
The world's political powers ultimately destroy the very culture of luxury and idolatry they supported; evil devours itself.
For those who identify Babylon with Rome, it pictures a returning Nero with eastern allies destroying Rome, a symbol of the self-destruction of empire (Bauckham, Aune).

symbols.phrase: God has put it into their hearts to carry out His purpose
symbols.jewish: God uses pagan powers as instruments of judgment: Assyria the rod of his anger (Isaiah 10:5-7), Nebuchadnezzar "my servant" (Jeremiah 25:9), Cyrus his anointed (Isaiah 45:1). He hardened Pharaoh's heart (Exodus 9:12) and moves the hearts of kings (Proverbs 21:1).
symbols.meaning: God's sovereignty extends even over the alliance of evil: its unity and its self-destruction both serve his purpose until his words are fulfilled.

symbols.phrase: The woman is the great city that rules over the kings of the earth
symbols.jewish: "The great city" is Jerusalem in Revelation 11:8 ("where their Lord was crucified") and Babylon in 14:8; 16:19; 18:10, 16, 18, 19, 21. Jeremiah 22:8 calls Jerusalem "this great city"; Jonah calls Nineveh "that great city" (Jonah 1:2). Lamentations 1:1 calls Jerusalem "great among the nations" and "princess among the provinces".
symbols.cultural: In John's time only Rome ruled over the kings of the earth in an obvious sense; client kings like Herod Agrippa held their thrones at Rome's pleasure.
symbols.meaning: The final explanation identifies the woman as a city with dominion over the world's rulers. For most interpreters it settles the matter in favour of Rome (or a future world capital); preterists who favour Jerusalem read the rule as covenantal or religious.

readings.reading: Gentry argues that Jerusalem held a covenantal kingship over the nations as the city of the great King (Psalm 48:2) and was the centre of the Jewish world; Chilton translates "kings of the land". Critics answer that the plain sense of rule over the kings of the earth fits Rome far better; preterists reply that 11:8 already defines "the great city" as Jerusalem.
Papal Rome, which in the Middle Ages claimed authority over the kings of Christendom, crowning and deposing them.
A future world capital, either a rebuilt Babylon or a revived Rome, ruling the nations in the last days.
The world city of every age, whose cultural and economic power holds sway over the rulers of the earth.
Rome, the ruling city of John's world, and its successors (Bauckham, Koester, Beale).

Gentry, Chilton, DeMar and others hold that the harlot is first-century Jerusalem and the beast is Rome. The harlot's priestly colours, her guilt for the blood of the prophets, her alliance with Rome (sitting on the beast) and her destruction by Rome in AD 70 all fit Jerusalem, and she is set against the New Jerusalem, the Bride. The seven kings are the Julio-Claudian emperors with Nero as the sixth, which supports a pre-70 date. Some other preterists and many early-date scholars instead identify Babylon with Rome and read the chapter as predicting Rome's judgment.

Shares the Jerusalem identification and sees the fall of the harlot in AD 70 as the end of the old covenant age and the marriage of the Lamb to the new covenant bride (Preston, King). Critics note this view collapses the future consummation into AD 70, against the historic creeds; proponents say the imminence language of Revelation requires it.

Babylon is papal Rome, the apostate church of the city on seven hills that ruled the kings of Europe and shed the blood of the martyrs. The beast is the Roman power in its papal phase, the ten horns are the barbarian kingdoms that succeeded Rome, and the beast's turning on the harlot is the gradual stripping of papal power by the nations (Luther, the Reformers, Newton, Elliott, Barnes).

The chapter describes the end time. Walvoord identifies the harlot with a future apostate world religion that supports and then is destroyed by the Antichrist and his ten-nation confederation; others (Dyer, Woods, Thomas) see a literal rebuilt Babylon in Iraq. The seven heads are successive world empires and the eighth the Antichrist's kingdom. Historic premillennialists (Ladd) see an end-time manifestation of the Rome-like world power.

Babylon is the world as seductress in every age, the culture of luxury, power and false religion that draws people from God, while the beast is persecuting political power. Rome was the form both took in John's day. Their mutual destruction shows that evil is self-defeating (Hendriksen, Milligan).

Most modern commentators (Bauckham, Aune, Koester, Beale, Osborne) see Rome as the first referent: the city on seven hills, the world ruler and the city Jewish writers called Babylon. The chapter also exposes a recurring pattern that will reach a final form at the end; the Nero redivivus legend shapes the riddle of the beast.

questions: List the clues in chapter 17 that point to Rome and those that point to Jerusalem. Which do you find strongest, and why?
Why does John portray Babylon as a prostitute and the New Jerusalem as a bride? What does the contrast teach about the church's relation to its culture?
How does the riddle of the seven kings (17:10) bear on the date of Revelation? Is it possible to count the kings with confidence?
What does it mean that the beast and the ten kings turn on the prostitute (17:16), and that God put it in their hearts (17:17)?
In what ways might "Babylon" be present in the economic and political life of today's world, whichever historical identification is correct?

title: The Fall of Babylon: Laments of Kings, Merchants and Sailors
summary: A glorious angel announces that Babylon the great has fallen and become a haunt of demons and unclean creatures, because the nations, kings and merchants were intoxicated and enriched by her. Another voice calls God's people to come out of her, and calls for her to be repaid double for her pride and luxury, since she boasted she sat as a queen and would never mourn. Three groups who profited from her stand at a distance and lament: the kings of the earth, the merchants, whose long cargo list catalogues the luxuries of the world ending with human beings, and the shipmasters and sailors. Heaven, the saints, apostles and prophets are told to rejoice, and a mighty angel hurls a millstone into the sea as a sign that the city will be thrown down and silenced: no music, craft, mill, lamp or wedding. Her guilt is her sorcery and the blood of prophets, saints and all the slain.

outline.heading: An angel of glory announces Babylon's fall
Come out of her, my people; repay her double; her boast and sudden judgment
The kings' lament
The merchants' lament and the cargo list
The sailors' lament
Call for heaven and the saints to rejoice
The millstone sign and the silencing of the city

context:
Revelation 18 is composed almost entirely of echoes of the prophets' oracles against Babylon and Tyre: Isaiah 13-14, 21 and 47; Jeremiah 50-51; and Ezekiel 26-28, Tyre's fall and the laments of kings, merchants and seamen. The cargo list (18:12-13) adapts Ezekiel 27:12-24, Tyre's trade list, and the millstone sign adapts Jeremiah 51:63-64, where Seraiah throws the scroll of Babylon's doom, tied to a stone, into the Euphrates. The silencing of music, mills, lamps and weddings repeats Jeremiah 25:10 (and 7:34; 16:9), words first spoken against Jerusalem and Judah. The structure is a funeral dirge (Hebrew qinah) in prophetic form, with the triple "Woe, woe" and the refrain "in one hour". Taunt-songs over fallen cities were a prophetic genre (Isaiah 14:4-21; Ezekiel 27).

Richard Bauckham's study "The Economic Critique of Rome in Revelation 18" (in The Climax of Prophecy) showed how closely the cargo list matches Rome's luxury imports: silk from China, citron wood from North Africa, ivory, cinnamon and spices via the Red Sea and India trade, Tyrian purple, marble and enormous imports of grain and slaves. Roman moralists such as Pliny the Elder complained of the drain of wealth to the East for luxuries (Natural History 6.101; 12.84) and of the craze for citron-wood tables (13.91-102). The lamenters are those who profited from the empire's economy: client kings, traders and shipowners, while the slave trade, "bodies and souls of human beings", stands at the end of the list as an indictment. Those who read Babylon as Jerusalem point instead to the wealth of the Herodian temple and its trade in sacrificial goods, priestly fabrics and incense, and to Jesus' words that the blood of the prophets would be required of Jerusalem. Futurists see a literal future commercial capital. The chapter's call to "come out of her" made it a text for Christian separation from compromised economic and religious systems throughout church history.

symbols.phrase: Another angel with great authority; the earth illuminated by his glory
symbols.jewish: Ezekiel 43:2 describes the glory of the God of Israel returning to the temple so that the earth shone with his glory. Angels reflecting God's glory appear in Daniel 10:6 and Luke 2:9.
symbols.meaning: The angel comes directly from God's presence, so the announcement carries divine authority. The glory that fills the earth contrasts with the darkness that will settle on Babylon (18:23).

symbols.phrase: Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great!
symbols.jewish: Isaiah 21:9: "Fallen, fallen is Babylon, and all the images of her gods are shattered." Jeremiah 51:8 says Babylon has suddenly fallen. The cry first appears in Revelation 14:8. The prophetic past tense ("has fallen") treats a future event as certain.
symbols.cultural: Historical Babylon was taken by Cyrus in 539 BC and later declined into ruins; by John's time it was largely deserted.
symbols.meaning: A proclamation of certain judgment, using the "prophetic perfect". It announces in advance what the rest of the chapter describes.

readings.reading: The fall of Jerusalem in AD 70 (Gentry, Chilton), or, for preterists who identify Babylon with Rome, the judgments on Rome beginning with the crisis of AD 68-69.
The final overthrow of papal Rome, in some readings literally by fire (Elliott, Barnes).
The future destruction of the end-time city (a rebuilt Babylon or revived Rome) at the end of the tribulation (Walvoord, Thomas).
The certain doom of the world system, anticipated in every fallen empire and completed at the end of history.

symbols.phrase: A lair for demons, a haunt for every unclean spirit, bird and beast
symbols.jewish: Prophetic oracles describe ruined Babylon and Edom as inhabited by desert creatures, owls, jackals, goat-demons (se'irim) and the night creature Lilith (Isaiah 13:19-22; 34:11-15; Jeremiah 50:39; 51:37). Baruch 4:35 threatens Babylon with demons. Unclean birds are those forbidden in Leviticus 11:13-19.
symbols.cultural: Ruined cities overgrown and home to wild animals were a familiar sight in the ancient world; Babylon itself had become such a place.
symbols.meaning: Total desolation. The city that hosted luxury now hosts only unclean spirits: the opposite of the New Jerusalem, into which nothing unclean enters (21:27).

symbols.phrase: All the nations have drunk the wine of the passion of her immorality
symbols.jewish: Jeremiah 51:7 and 25:15-16: Babylon's cup made the nations mad. "Passion" (Greek thymos) can mean both passion and wrath, a wordplay: her intoxicating wine becomes God's wrath (14:8, 10).
symbols.meaning: The nations were intoxicated by what Babylon offered: power, wealth and idolatry. The wordplay hints that her seduction carries its own punishment.

symbols.phrase: The merchants of the earth grew rich from the extravagance of her luxury
symbols.jewish: Ezekiel 27-28 portrays Tyre as a merchant city whose trade led to pride and violence (Ezekiel 28:5, 16). Isaiah 23:8 calls Tyre's merchants princes. Ezekiel 27:33 says Tyre enriched the kings of the earth.
symbols.cultural: Merchants (emporoi) were long-distance wholesale traders. Rome was the greatest market of the ancient world, and trading guilds in cities such as Thyatira and Laodicea were tied to civic and imperial cults, which made participation a problem for Christians (Revelation 2:20).
symbols.meaning: Babylon's guilt includes an economic system that enriches traders through luxury. Bauckham argues that Revelation's critique is economic as well as religious and political.

readings.reading: The merchants who traded with Jerusalem and its temple, whose wealth Josephus describes (Chilton).
Global commerce centred on the end-time commercial capital.
A permanent warning about economic systems that serve luxury and exploit people.

symbols.phrase: Come out of her, My people
symbols.jewish: The prophets commanded the exiles to leave Babylon: Jeremiah 50:8; 51:6, 45 ("Go out of her, my people"); Isaiah 48:20; 52:11 (quoted in 2 Corinthians 6:17). Lot was told to flee Sodom (Genesis 19:12-22). Jesus told disciples in Judea to flee to the mountains when they saw Jerusalem surrounded (Luke 21:20-21).
symbols.cultural: Christians in the cities of Asia faced pressure to join trade-guild banquets, civic festivals and imperial-cult celebrations to keep their livelihood.
symbols.meaning: A call to separate from Babylon's sins so as not to share her plagues. Many interpreters understand it as moral and spiritual separation (refusing compromise) rather than geographic flight, though the latter is possible.

readings.reading: Christians fled Jerusalem before the siege; Eusebius reports that the Jerusalem church, warned by an oracle, moved to Pella (Ecclesiastical History 3.5.3).
A call to leave the Roman church, cited by the Reformers and later Protestants as a mandate for separation.
A literal call to believers in the end-time city to leave before its destruction.
A permanent call to refuse complicity with the world's idolatry and exploitation while living within it.

symbols.phrase: Her sins are piled up to heaven, and God has remembered her iniquities
symbols.jewish: Jeremiah 51:9: Babylon's judgment reaches to heaven. The builders of Babel wanted a tower reaching to heaven (Genesis 11:4); Ezra 9:6 speaks of guilt mounting to the heavens.
symbols.meaning: The image may echo the tower of Babel: her sins form a tower to heaven, and God, who seemed to forget, now remembers.

symbols.phrase: Pay her back double; mix her a double portion in her own cup
symbols.jewish: Jeremiah 16:18 and 17:18 speak of double repayment for sin; Jeremiah 50:15, 29 calls for Babylon to be repaid as she has done. Isaiah 40:2 says Jerusalem has received double for her sins. Exodus 22:4, 7, 9 requires a thief to repay double.
symbols.meaning: The point is full and fitting retribution. Some scholars (for example Meredith Kline) argue the Greek diplosate means "repay the equivalent" (a matching duplicate) rather than twice as much, which fits the principle "as she has done".

symbols.phrase: I sit as queen; I am not a widow and will never see grief
symbols.jewish: Isaiah 47:7-9 is the source: Babylon says she will be mistress forever and will never be a widow or lose children, but both will come in one day. By contrast, Lamentations 1:1 mourns Jerusalem as "like a widow". Tyre's pride is condemned in Ezekiel 28:2.
symbols.cultural: Rome was personified as the goddess Roma, often enthroned on coins, and celebrated as Roma Aeterna, the eternal city.
symbols.meaning: Self-glorification and the illusion of permanent security. Her proud self-confidence is exactly what will be overturned.

readings.reading: Jerusalem's confidence in the temple and her covenant status (Jeremiah 7:4; Matthew 3:9), refusing to see herself as a widow while she rejected her husband (Chilton).
Rome's ideology of eternal rule, Roma Aeterna (Bauckham, Koester).
The arrogance of the end-time city at the height of its power.

symbols.phrase: Her plagues will come in one day: death, grief, famine; consumed by fire
symbols.jewish: Isaiah 47:9 ("both will come in a moment, in one day"). Babylon fell to the Persians in a single night (Daniel 5:30). Fire was the fate of Sodom (Genesis 19:24) and, in the law, of a prostitute priest's daughter (Leviticus 21:9); compare 17:16.
symbols.cultural: Sieges brought death, mourning and famine together; Josephus describes the horrors of famine in besieged Jerusalem (Jewish War 5.424-438; 6.193-213).
symbols.meaning: Sudden, total destruction, in contrast to her sense of permanence. "Mighty is the Lord God who judges her" shows that no city is too strong for God.

readings.reading: Pestilence, mourning, famine and fire describe the siege of Jerusalem and its burning in AD 70 (Chilton, Gentry).
Some historicists expected a literal burning of Rome as the final end of the papacy (Elliott).
A literal sudden destruction of the end-time city, perhaps in a single day.

symbols.phrase: The kings of the earth weep and wail, standing at a distance: Woe, woe, the great city
symbols.jewish: Ezekiel 26:15-18 and 27:35 describe the princes and kings of the coastlands trembling and lamenting over Tyre. The lament form (qinah) appears in Lamentations and Ezekiel 27. The double "woe" (Greek ouai ouai) is a funeral cry.
symbols.cultural: Client kings depended on Rome for their thrones and wealth; the end of Rome would be the end of their own position.
symbols.meaning: The kings mourn not for the city but for what they have lost; they stand at a distance because they fear sharing her fate. Their lament is self-interested.

symbols.phrase: In a single hour your judgment has come
symbols.jewish: Isaiah 47:9, 11 (suddenly, in one day); Daniel 5:30. The ten kings rule "one hour" with the beast (17:12).
symbols.meaning: The refrain repeated by each group stresses the shocking speed of the fall. It echoes the "one hour" of the beast's allies: their brief hour of power is matched by the city's sudden hour of judgment.

symbols.phrase: The cargo: gold, silver, precious stones and pearls, fine linen, purple, silk and scarlet
symbols.jewish: Ezekiel 27:12-24 lists Tyre's trade with the nations by region and product; Revelation's list of 28 or 29 items (a multiple of seven, by some counts) adapts it. Many items were also materials of the tabernacle and temple (Exodus 25:3-7; 35:5-9).
symbols.cultural: Bauckham shows that nearly every item was a prized import to Rome: gold and silver for display, gems and pearls (Pliny calls pearls the most costly of all things, Natural History 9.106), fine linen from Egypt, purple dye from Tyre, silk from China (worth its weight in gold), scarlet from kermes. Pliny estimated that India, China and Arabia drained the empire of 100 million sesterces a year (Natural History 12.84).
symbols.meaning: The list displays the luxury that fed one city's appetite at the cost of the provinces and the poor. It moves from precious materials to food and finally to human beings, exposing the moral cost of the system.

readings.reading: Chilton and others note how many of the goods were used in the temple and its sacrifices (gold, purple, scarlet, fine linen, incense, spices, flour, oil, wine, cattle and sheep), suggesting Jerusalem's temple economy; critics answer that silk, ivory, citron wood, marble and the slave trade fit Rome far better (Bauckham), while preterists reply that the list is modelled on Ezekiel 27's lament over Tyre and so need not be an inventory of the city's own imports.
The wealth and trade of the papal church, including the sale of offices, relics and indulgences (Barnes).
The worldwide trade of a literal end-time commercial capital.
A portrait of consumer luxury in every civilisation that worships wealth.

symbols.phrase: All kinds of citron wood, articles of ivory, precious wood, bronze, iron and marble
symbols.jewish: Ivory and fine woods adorned Solomon's palace and throne (1 Kings 10:18-22); Amos condemned the rich of Samaria for "houses of ivory" (Amos 3:15; 6:4). Ezekiel 27:15 lists ivory traded by Tyre.
symbols.cultural: Citron wood (thyine wood, from the North African thuja tree) was the most fashionable timber in Rome; tables made from its grained roots sold for the price of an estate (Pliny, Natural History 13.91-102). Ivory came from Africa and India in great quantities for furniture and statues; coloured marble was quarried across the empire, and Augustus boasted that he found Rome a city of brick and left it of marble (Suetonius, Augustus 28).
symbols.meaning: The fittings of elite Roman houses and public buildings. These items are hard to connect with Jerusalem and are among the strongest clues for a Roman setting.

symbols.phrase: Cinnamon, spice, incense, myrrh and frankincense
symbols.jewish: Cinnamon, myrrh and frankincense were ingredients of the holy anointing oil and incense of the tabernacle (Exodus 30:23-38). The magi brought frankincense and myrrh to Jesus (Matthew 2:11). Proverbs 7:17 has the adulteress perfume her bed with myrrh and cinnamon.
symbols.cultural: Spices came by caravan from Arabia and by sea from India and Sri Lanka; the Greek amomon was an Indian aromatic used in perfumes and funeral rites. Incense burned at every pagan altar and in the imperial cult.
symbols.meaning: The perfumes of luxury, worship and seduction. For some readers, their link to the temple suggests Jerusalem; for others, their role in pagan cult and Roman banquets suggests Rome.

readings.reading: Incense and spices for the Jerusalem temple, a major element of its economy (Chilton).
Imports for Roman perfumes, banquets, funerals and pagan temples (Bauckham).

symbols.phrase: Wine, olive oil, fine flour and wheat; cattle, sheep, horses and chariots
symbols.jewish: Fine flour, oil and wine were offerings in the temple (Leviticus 2:1-7; Numbers 15:4-10); cattle and sheep were sacrificial animals. Solomon imported horses and chariots (1 Kings 10:28-29), which Deuteronomy 17:16 forbade kings to multiply. Compare the third seal's prices of wheat, oil and wine (Revelation 6:6).
symbols.cultural: Rome imported vast quantities of grain from Egypt and North Africa for its free grain dole; fine flour (similis) was a luxury for the wealthy. The Greek word for chariot here (rhede) denotes a four-wheeled carriage of the rich.
symbols.meaning: Even staples flowed to the capital, and luxury carriages marked the elite. Bauckham notes that Rome's grain supply sometimes left provinces short.

symbols.phrase: Slaves and souls of men
symbols.jewish: Ezekiel 27:13 says Javan, Tubal and Meshech traded "the souls of men" (human beings) with Tyre. Joel 3:3-6 condemns Tyre and Sidon for selling Judeans as slaves. The law condemned kidnapping and selling a person (Exodus 21:16; Deuteronomy 24:7; 1 Timothy 1:10).
symbols.cultural: The Greek is literally "bodies, and souls of human beings". "Bodies" (somata) was the trade term for slaves in markets and sale documents. Rome's economy depended on millions of slaves, many from conquest; after the Jewish War Josephus says 97,000 captives were taken (Jewish War 6.420).
symbols.meaning: The list ends with human beings, treated as merchandise. The addition "and souls of human beings" may be John's protest: slaves are not mere bodies but persons. It is the climax of the economic critique.

readings.reading: Some preterists see it as the trade in people that accompanied Jerusalem's fall and its own exploitation of the poor; others accept that the slave trade points to Rome.
A lasting indictment of every economy that treats human beings as commodities, including modern trafficking.

symbols.phrase: The fruit of your soul's desire has departed; your luxury and splendour have vanished
symbols.jewish: Compare the rich fool of Luke 12:16-21 and James 5:1-5 (the rich whose riches have rotted). Ezekiel 27:27 lists Tyre's wealth sinking into the sea.
symbols.meaning: An aside addressed directly to the city: what she craved is gone forever. The repeated "never again" (Greek ou me) begins here and continues to 18:23.

symbols.phrase: The merchants weep and mourn: clothed in fine linen and purple and scarlet
symbols.jewish: Ezekiel 27:31-36 records the merchants of the nations hissing and wailing over Tyre. The description of the city in 18:16 repeats the harlot's clothing in 17:4.
symbols.cultural: Merchants and their guilds were among the main beneficiaries of Roman peace and markets.
symbols.meaning: The merchants grieve over lost profits: they repeat the city's finery as if mourning a lost customer. The city and the harlot are clearly one.

symbols.phrase: Every shipmaster, passenger and sailor stood at a distance; they threw dust on their heads
symbols.jewish: Ezekiel 27:28-34: Tyre's pilots and sailors stand on the shore, throw dust on their heads, roll in ashes and cry "Who was ever destroyed like Tyre?" Throwing dust is a sign of mourning (Joshua 7:6; Job 2:12; Lamentations 2:10).
symbols.cultural: Rome depended on shipping, especially the grain fleets from Alexandria and the port of Ostia (and Puteoli). Shipowners were a powerful commercial class; Claudius gave them incentives to keep grain flowing (Suetonius, Claudius 18-19).
symbols.meaning: Maritime trade wept over the loss of its greatest market. Their cry "What city was ever like this great city?" echoes Ezekiel 27:32 and parodies the praise of God ("Who is like the beast?" in 13:4; "Who is like you, O LORD?" in Exodus 15:11).

readings.reading: Gentry and Chilton argue Jerusalem's commerce and pilgrim trade reached across the Mediterranean; critics answer that a seaborne trade centre fits Rome better.
Global shipping tied to the future capital.

symbols.phrase: Rejoice over her, O heaven, O saints and apostles and prophets
symbols.jewish: Jeremiah 51:48: the heavens and the earth will shout for joy over Babylon. Deuteronomy 32:43 calls the heavens to rejoice when God avenges his servants' blood. The legal language ("God has judged your judgment against her") suggests a court verdict in favour of the saints.
symbols.meaning: The saints rejoice not out of revenge but because God has vindicated them in a lawsuit. The mention of apostles places the persecution in the apostolic era for many interpreters.

readings.reading: The apostles and prophets killed by Jerusalem's leaders (Stephen, James son of Zebedee, James the Just) are vindicated in AD 70.
Peter and Paul, by tradition martyred in Rome under Nero, are among those vindicated (Bauckham, Koester).
The redeemed in heaven rejoice at the final fall of the end-time system.

symbols.phrase: A mighty angel cast a stone like a great millstone into the sea
symbols.jewish: Jeremiah 51:63-64: Seraiah ties a stone to the scroll of Babylon's doom and throws it into the Euphrates, saying Babylon will sink and rise no more. Exodus 15:5 says Pharaoh's army sank like a stone. Jesus said it would be better for one who causes little ones to stumble to have a millstone hung around the neck and be thrown into the sea (Matthew 18:6); and he spoke of a mountain being cast into the sea (Matthew 21:21).
symbols.cultural: A "great millstone" (mylos onikos) was the large stone turned by a donkey in commercial mills.
symbols.meaning: A prophetic sign-act: sudden, violent and irreversible destruction. Some preterists connect "this mountain" cast into the sea (Matthew 21:21, said near the temple mount) with Jerusalem.

readings.reading: Jerusalem thrown down in AD 70, never to be the centre of God's covenant worship again; some link it to Jesus' word about "this mountain" being cast into the sea (Chilton).
The final, total destruction of the end-time city.
The certain and permanent end of the godless world order.

symbols.phrase: No more harpists, flute players, trumpeters, craftsmen or the sound of a millstone
symbols.jewish: Jeremiah 25:10 (against Judah and Jerusalem) and 7:34; 16:9 speak of God silencing the sounds of joy, of bride and bridegroom, of millstones and the light of the lamp. Ezekiel 26:13 silences Tyre's songs and harps. Isaiah 24:8 ends the joy of tambourines and lyres.
symbols.cultural: Music accompanied banquets, festivals, weddings and funerals in Roman cities; trade guilds of craftsmen were central to urban life and civic religion.
symbols.meaning: The ordinary sounds of a living city fall silent: culture, work and daily bread. The repeated "never again" is a funeral knell. In contrast, heaven is filled with music (19:1-8).

readings.reading: Jeremiah 25:10 was spoken against Jerusalem; preterists see the same judgment repeated on the city in AD 70.

symbols.phrase: No light of a lamp; no voice of bride and bridegroom
symbols.jewish: Jeremiah 7:34; 16:9; 25:10; 33:11 (the voice of bride and bridegroom will return to restored Jerusalem). Lamps lit wedding processions (Matthew 25:1-13).
symbols.meaning: Home life and future generations end. The silence of the human wedding in Babylon prepares for the joyous wedding of the Lamb and his Bride (19:7-9) and for the city that needs no lamp because God is its light (21:23; 22:5).

symbols.phrase: Your merchants were the great ones of the earth; all nations were deceived by your sorcery
symbols.jewish: Isaiah 23:8 calls Tyre's merchants princes; Isaiah 47:9, 12 condemns Babylon's many sorceries and spells; Nahum 3:4 calls Nineveh "mistress of sorceries" who sold nations. Sorcery (pharmakeia) is listed among the sins of the unrepentant (Revelation 9:21; 21:8; 22:15).
symbols.cultural: Magic, astrology and drugs (pharmaka) were widespread in the Greco-Roman world; Ephesus was famous for magical books (Acts 19:19). "Great ones" (megistanes) were the magnates and courtiers of the empire.
symbols.meaning: Two charges: arrogance of the merchant class, and deceptive enchantment of the nations. Babylon's "sorcery" is the spell of wealth and power that blinded the world.

symbols.phrase: In her was found the blood of prophets and saints, and of all slain on the earth
symbols.jewish: Jeremiah 51:49: Babylon must fall for the slain of Israel, as the slain of all the earth fell because of Babylon. Jesus said that on Jerusalem would come all the righteous blood shed on earth, from Abel to Zechariah (Matthew 23:35-37), and that a prophet cannot perish outside Jerusalem (Luke 13:33-34).
symbols.cultural: Rome's wars and executions, including Nero's killing of Christians in AD 64, made it the great shedder of blood in the Mediterranean world.
symbols.meaning: The final verdict: Babylon is guilty not only of the blood of God's servants but of all violent death on earth. The scope is universal.

readings.reading: Gentry and Chilton see this as the decisive echo of Matthew 23:35 and Luke 13:33: the city guilty of the blood of the prophets is Jerusalem. Critics reply that the phrase "all who were slain on the earth" fits an imperial power better, and that Jeremiah 51:49 is the closer source; preterists answer that Jesus himself laid on Jerusalem "all the righteous blood shed on earth" (Matthew 23:35).
Papal Rome, accused of shedding the blood of martyrs over many centuries.
Every violent world power is guilty of the blood shed by the system it represents.
Rome, and every persecuting empire that follows its pattern (Bauckham, Beale).

Gentry, Chilton and others read the chapter as a dirge over first-century Jerusalem. "Come out of her" matches the flight of Christians to Pella; plagues, famine and fire match the siege of AD 70; the cargo list includes the materials and sacrificial goods of the temple economy; the silencing of bride and bridegroom repeats Jeremiah 25:10, spoken against Jerusalem; and the blood of the prophets is the charge Jesus laid on Jerusalem (Matthew 23:35). Preterists who identify Babylon with Rome read the chapter as a prophecy of Rome's judgment, beginning with the upheavals of AD 68-69.

The fall of Jerusalem in AD 70 was the decisive judgment that ended the old covenant world and cleared the way for the wedding of the Lamb in 19:7-9 (Preston, King). Critics observe that this leaves no future consummation of the kind confessed in the historic creeds; proponents reply that Scripture's time indicators bind the fulfilment to that generation.

Babylon is papal Rome, whose final destruction (in some accounts by literal fire) is still future or in progress; the call to "come out of her" was the Reformation's summons to leave Rome; the cargo list reflects the wealth and trade of the medieval church (Elliott, Barnes; earlier the Reformers and Puritans).

The chapter describes the literal destruction of an end-time commercial and political capital at the close of the tribulation. Dyer, Woods and Thomas expect a rebuilt Babylon on the Euphrates, since Isaiah 13 and Jeremiah 50-51 were not, in their view, fully fulfilled; Walvoord distinguishes the religious Babylon of chapter 17 (destroyed by the beast) from the commercial Babylon of chapter 18 (destroyed by God).

Babylon is the world as economic and cultural seductress in every age. The laments of the kings, merchants and sailors show how dependent societies become on wealth and luxury, and the call to come out of her is a permanent summons to Christians to refuse complicity (Hendriksen, Milligan).

Bauckham's influential reading sees chapter 18 as a prophetic critique of Rome's economy, built from the oracles against Babylon and Tyre, which also stands as a pattern for every exploitative world power until the final judgment. Beale, Koester and Osborne broadly agree.

questions: Which items in the cargo list point most clearly to Rome, and which could fit Jerusalem's temple economy? How much weight should the list carry in identifying Babylon?
The kings, merchants and sailors mourn from a distance. What does their lament reveal about what they loved?
How should Christians today hear the command "Come out of her, my people" (18:4)? Is it a call to physical separation, moral distance or both?
Why does the list end with "bodies and souls of human beings"? What does that say about God's judgment on economic systems?
How does the silence of Babylon (18:22-23) prepare for the wedding of the Lamb and the New Jerusalem?
